turns.zh: 是啊，莱尼，很高兴再次邀请您加入。能来这里我很兴奋，也很期待能与大家分享心得。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The reason I'm excited to have you back on the podcast is because I've heard from so many listeners that they're either struggling to find a job in this market or hate the job that they're in. They're not sure what to do about it. Or on the flip side, they're trying to hire amazing people or keep amazing people and they're having a hard time doing that. And luckily you just wrote a new book called Job Moves that I have right here that has a very different set of advice and different perspective on how to approach these problems. And if I may, the job to be done of this episode is to help people find a job that they love, find a better job, decide when to leave a job and hire and keep amazing people. How's that sound?
turns.zh: 我特别期待您能重返播客，是因为我从许多听众那里听说，他们要么在这个市场上找不到工作，或者对现有工作心怀不满，不知道该如何改变现状；要么他们正努力招聘优秀人才或留住现有员工，却屡屡碰壁。幸运的是，您刚出版了一本新书《Job Moves》，我手头就有一本，书中为解决这些问题提供了截然不同的建议和视角。如果可以的话，本期节目的核心任务就是帮助人们找到热爱的工作、提升职业发展、掌握离职时机，以及成功招聘和留住优秀人才。您觉得怎么样？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah. The premise of this was I've been asking founders for 15 years, what are the top three things that you really... If you could wave a magic wand and solve, what would it be? And talent was always on that list. And to be honest, I really didn't want to go into the space because it's just so... I don't know, to me it was icky, but at the same time, the reality is I realized there's just a lot of struggling moments around it and for me and what I do, I just love to help struggling moments. And so it started out almost 15 years ago working with Ethan Bernstein, who's a business school professor at Harvard in the organizational behavior side. And basically, he saw me do an interview around jobs for a product and said, "Well, boy, I think we should think about this for..." Because I'm giving advice to students about what they should do in their next career or their next job. (00:06:48): And he's like, "Could we modify this?" And so over the last 15 years we've interviewed over a thousand people. I've coached almost a thousand people. We've built a class around it and it's one of those things that I've become... Like I went down the rabbit hole and I couldn't get out. And so it's very, very exciting. And to be honest, the book launched in November and I think that ultimately I'll be remembered more for this book than Jobs-to-be-Done because I think there's a billion people a year who switch jobs and ultimately most of them end up with a job that's worse than the one they were at, but they don't know how to find it and part of it is they don't know themselves well enough. And so I've just learned so much and I'm excited to be here to share all the little insights that I've learned along the way.
turns.zh: 是的。这个项目的初衷是，过去15年来我一直在问创业者们：你们最需要解决的三大难题是什么？如果能挥动魔法棒一举解决，那会是什么？人才问题始终位列其中。说实话，我起初并不想涉足这个领域，因为它实在太……我不知道怎么说，但对我而言这感觉挺恶心的。但现实是，我意识到围绕人才问题存在诸多困境，而对于我所做的工作，我就是乐于帮助人们克服这些难题。于是15年前，我开始与哈佛商学院组织行为学教授伊桑·伯恩斯坦合作。当时他看到我为产品职位做采访时谈到，"嗯，小子，咱们得好好考虑这个问题。"因为我当时正为学生们提供职业规划建议，告诉他们下一份工作该如何选择。（00:06:48）他问："能不能对这个模型进行改进？"过去15年间，我们采访了上千人，指导了近千人。我们围绕这个主题开发了课程，如今它已成为我深陷其中的热爱事业。非常令人兴奋的是，这本书11月刚出版，我相信最终人们记住我的会更多是因为这本书，而非"待完成工作"理论——毕竟每年有10亿人换工作，其中多数最终得到的工作比原先更差，但他们不知道如何找到更好的机会。通过这些研究，我收获颇丰，很高兴能在此分享一路走来积累的点滴见解。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was going to say that there's a high bar you have to hit for this to be more impactful than Jobs-to-be-Done. I love that you believe it will be.
turns.zh: 我原本想说要让这个项目比"待完成工作"理论更有影响力，你得达到很高的标准。不过我很欣慰你对此充满信心。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Oh, yeah. Well, I think there's only a small group. I actually think your audience really appreciates Jobs-to-be-Done, but I think the fact is that there's only... Let's say there's a hundred thousand people who need to know Jobs-to-be-Done. There are a billion people every year who actually need to know how to find their next job. And so to me, it's just a much bigger market. And so that's why I think I'll have more impact on it.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得受众群体很有限。其实我觉得听众们都很欣赏"待完成工作"理论，但现实是，真正需要了解这个理论的人只有……比如说有十万人需要了解"待完成工作"理论，但每年有10亿人需要知道如何找到下一份工作。对我而言，后者市场要大得多。这就是为什么我认为自己能产生更大的影响力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And it also helps people hiring. So the TAM is even larger.
turns.zh: 是的。这对招聘方也有帮助。所以潜在市场规模更大。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: The thing that I've learned though is that Jobs-to-be-Done is a very powerful concept, but the reality is I think it's actually more beneficial when you apply it to things. So I've applied it to sales, I've applied it to college, I've applied it to careers, and so part of it is figuring out where to apply it next. And so I have other places that I'm working on, but the reality is I think jobs is so powerful that it will just help recreate categories.
turns.zh: 不过我学到的一点是，"待完成工作"理论是个非常强大的概念，但实际上，当你将其应用于具体事物时会更有价值。比如我把它应用于销售、大学教育、职业规划等领域，接下来要考虑的是在哪些领域继续深化应用。我还有其他方向在探索，但我认为工作这个领域潜力巨大，将重塑整个行业。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So before I get into specific questions and tactics that you share in the book, what's just the big idea behind this book and that would be helpful for people to understand as we get into the tactics?
turns.zh: 好的。在深入探讨书中具体策略和方法之前，能否先讲讲这本书的核心理念？这对理解后续策略会很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: The number one thing we heard that when you do these interviews is the first thing they say, "Well, tell me about your new job." They go like, "Oh my God, I got so lucky." They just attributed it all to luck. And ultimately luck is when opportunity meets preparedness. And so you start to realize that when you start to interview people about the luck, it turns out that there was things that happened to them that made them ready to see the opportunity. And there's other things where actually their experiences actually shaped what they were looking for and so they could see the opportunity. And so you started to realize this is a much bigger thing around that employees hire companies more than companies hire employees. That's really the big thing. And if that's the case, how do I prepare you as an employee to know how to hire your job every single day, wherever you're at, how do you make sure you're doing the things you want to do and you're making progress in your life? Because the moment you stop making progress in your career is the moment you start looking for another job.
turns.zh: 关于面试时人们最常问的问题，第一句往往是：“嗯，跟我们讲讲你的新工作吧。”然后他们会感叹：“天哪，我真是太幸运了。”他们把成功完全归功于运气。但运气其实是机遇与准备的交集。当你深入探讨人们对运气的看法时，会发现那些成功者往往都经历了特定的准备阶段。有些人通过自身经历塑造了对机遇的敏锐感知，而另一些人则因准备不足而错失良机。这让我们深刻意识到，雇员选择公司远比公司选择雇员更为重要。既然如此，作为雇员，我们该如何做好准备，每天在工作中主动把握机遇，掌控职业生涯？因为当你职业发展停滞时，就是你在寻找新工作的时候了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And we're going to talk about the four quests of the jobs people have and all that stuff. But I want to get into something very specific and see where this conversation goes with that. And this is starting from a perspective of someone looking for a job and struggling to find a job. You have this really interesting distinction in the book between job features like salary and title and job experiences.
turns.zh: 好的。接下来我们会讨论人们在工作中面临的四个挑战，但我想先聚焦一个具体问题，看看我们能从中获得什么启发。这是从求职者视角出发的，他们在求职过程中遇到困难，苦苦挣扎。书中对职位特性（如薪资、头衔）和工作体验进行了有趣的区分。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Talk about what that is and why that's so important to understand.
turns.zh: 请解释一下这两者的区别，以及为什么理解它们如此重要。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Well, it's very similar to product. There's difference between product features and product experiences. And what you start to realize is that the experiences that keep you at your job and the good experiences and bad experiences are the things that actually pull it together, which is how attributes work through time and space. And so ultimately you want people to realize it's not just about the money, it's about is the money actually... Do they give you more money for a sign of respect? Because you start to realize when we did this, you'd unpack money. Money is a surrogate for respect or I've got bills to pay or I'm falling behind, or the fact is I deserve more. And so it comes back to money has actually many, many different implications to it and it's getting people to know why they want more money. Because everybody wants more money, but the question is why do you want more money? And that's really that understanding there. (00:10:48): So to me it's about actually understanding the experiences because you start to realize there's a concept we talk about and we'll probably get to about energy drivers and energy drains. So think of moments where you actually go into a situation and you get energy from it. Well, that's an experience that's not an attribute. At the same time, the fact this is those moments where you go in and you get the life sucked out of you, that's an experience. And so part of it is helping people understand the experiences they want so they can be successful, not the features.
turns.zh: 嗯，这和产品设计非常相似。产品特性（如薪资、头衔）和产品体验之间存在差异。你会发现，是那些让你留在职位上的经历——无论是好的还是坏的——最终决定了整体体验。这就是属性如何在时空中发挥作用的道理。归根结底，人们不只是看重钱，而是钱是否能传递尊重？因为我们发现，人们对钱的看法各不相同。有人认为钱是尊重的象征，有人是为了支付账单，有人是觉得自己配得上更多。所以钱的含义远不止于数字，关键在于让人们明白自己为什么想要更多钱。毕竟每个人都想赚更多钱，但问题是——你为什么想赚更多钱？这才是关键的洞察。（00:10:48）所以对我来说，关键在于理解这些体验，因为你会发现我们常提到的能量驱动因素和能量消耗因素。想想那些能给你带来活力的时刻。这些都是体验，而非属性。同时，那些让你精疲力竭的时刻同样是体验。所以关键在于帮助人们理解他们想要的体验，而非停留在表面特性上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's follow that thread of experiences, and this is a good segue to the four reasons people leave jobs and the quest as you described. So talk about what these experiences might be that you should be thinking about.
turns.zh: 那就沿着体验这条线索继续探讨吧。这也是过渡到你提到的四个离职原因和求职之道的绝佳契机。请谈谈人们应该关注的这些体验具体是什么。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: What we do is we do these interviews and we basically think of it as the ultimate of exit interviews. Why did you really leave this job? And so most of the time people won't tell their companies the truth. And so these are unfiltered interviews around like tell me what was really going on and out of it, we end up getting what we call pushes and pulls and these pushes and pulls is we end up with 13 different pushes. Things like I'm bored, things like I'm pushed beyond my ability, I've been disrespected. There's these things that have to happen that cause them to do that. There's also 14 pulls which is I want to work with a team that's got my back. I want to feel like I'm doing my best work. I want to make sure that I can free up time so I can carry my weight at home. (00:12:09): There's these other things that you pull for. But what happened is that when you start to look at all thousand interviews, they fall into one of four buckets. Two of them really are the standard thing. One is this bucket of get out. It is sucking my energy. I don't really know what to do, I can't think about what to do next. Help me get out of here so I can actually start to breathe and think. Right? Another quest is help me take the next step, which is I am where I am. The fact is I don't see a place where I can go next. And the fact is I want to take the next step to build some skills or capabilities, help me find that place where I can take my next step. Those are two standard ones, but what you start to realize is there's two others and the others are basically help me regain control. (00:12:51): This is where you like what you're doing, but the fact is that at some point there's just too much of it and you're not doing it in a way that basically you don't like the way you're doing it. And so part of it is pulling you back to basically where you actually have control over the work and control over yourself and control to basically manage your time yourself because at some point we get sucked in and it happens a lot in startups. It gets to be so much it's like, all right, I need to get control because my home life is falling apart. There's things like that and I can speak from experience on that where I've actually sold out of a startup so I could actually go back and fix my home life. There's the fourth one though is a very interesting one, which is when you're in a position and you start to end up... You end getting stretched into other places where you're not necessarily so good, but the fact is it is part of the experience, but you need to be realigned. (00:13:39): It's like help me realign back to the things that I'm really good at and what I like to do. And so ultimately you go into a position, you get a promotion, you end up moving to a place where you can see where it's there and all of a sudden you end up waking up one morning and going like, God, why am I doing all this stuff? I really like to do that stuff. I had this one, for example, I grew my firm where I had almost 50 people and I started to realize I spent all my time on people issues and I love to work on product. And so eventually I actually reshaped the whole business to get us down to five people. (00:14:12): I found everybody else jobs and then ultimately helped me basically get back to being able to do the work because that's the stuff I love to do. And so it's these four different quests that you realize. And what's interesting is if I look through my career, I've been in all four of those quests sometime in my life, and part of it is to assess your situation so you understand what quest you're on so you can actually start to understand what it's going to take to make the move that you need to make.
turns.zh:
我们的做法是进行这些访谈，我们基本上把它视为离职面谈的终极版本。为什么你真的要离开这份工作？大多数情况下，人们不会向公司说出真相。因此，这些未经过滤的访谈会让受访者畅谈真实经历，最终我们会得到所谓的“推力”和“拉力”分析。这些推力和拉力具体包括：比如“我感到无聊”、“我的能力被过度压榨”、“我受到了不尊重”等。这些问题背后必然存在导致员工离职的深层原因。此外，还有14种拉力因素，比如“我希望与支持我的团队共事”、“我渴望发挥最佳工作状态”、“我要确保能腾出时间兼顾家庭”等。（00:12:09）  
当我们分析数千份访谈时，会发现它们大致可归为四类。其中两类属于常见类型：一类是“逃离型”，即“这份工作耗尽了我的精力，我不知道该何去何从，请帮我离开这里”。另一类是“成长型”，即“我已达到现有职位上限，但看不到下一步的发展方向”或“我渴望提升技能，寻求职业突破”。  
最引人注目的是后两类，即“重获掌控型”和“重塑自我型”。前者源于人们在某个阶段被工作淹没，渴望回归能自主掌控工作的状态；后者则出于家庭压力，需要调整方向以兼顾工作与生活。  
（00:13:39）  
例如，某位高管在创业公司担任要职后，因精力耗尽而退出。还有人因晋升后被调任不擅长的领域，最终通过调整重回擅长领域。  
这些探索之旅最终指向四大核心诉求：  
1. 重获掌控：回归擅长领域，专注核心任务。  
2. 重塑自我：调整角色定位，重建职业方向。  
3. 重获成长：通过学习提升技能，突破职业瓶颈。  
4. 重构关系：在家庭与事业间找到平衡，构建和谐生态。
听着，我知道你现在很迷茫，但我需要你先冷静下来，仔细想想自己真正想要的是什么。别急着做决定，先了解一下实现目标需要付出什么样的努力，这样你才能真正明白接下来该怎么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was the beginning of the question I was about to ask, which is why this is so important. So why does someone need to spend time understanding what is pulling them to get out to leave?
turns.zh: 以上就是我接下来要提问的开头，这也是为什么这个问题如此重要。那么，为什么人们需要花时间去理解是什么在驱使他们离开现职呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: If I go back to Jobs to Done theory, its value is created by the context that you're in and the outcome that you want and you start to realize that through your life, your context changes. And so at some point, for example, in my twenties, I'd love to learn a lot of things. And so it was this whole notion of learning lots of things. But once I mastered it was like, all right, I know all these things. What can I do next? And so you start to realize that it's about that. (00:15:13): Where are you in this world and why is it creating that space for you to go like, "Yeah, what else can I do?" And what I would say is nobody randomly changes jobs, it's just not possible. And so the reality is you can describe it that way and most people would say Lucky is random, but the reality is it's caused and if it's now caused, you start to actually realize that context has a lot of impact in it because if I don't have enough context, I don't have enough pushes, I can complain about my job, but I'll never make the switch. So how many people say they want a new job, but they actually don't know what to do?
turns.zh: 如果回归到"工作完成理论"，其价值源于你所处的环境和期望的结果。你会意识到，人生中环境在不断变化。例如，在我二十多岁的时候，我渴望学习各种新知识，但一旦掌握了这些知识，人们就会问：接下来我能做什么？这时你才意识到，关键在于你身处何种境遇，又为何能创造出那种让你说“是啊，我还能做些什么”的空间。（00:15:13）：你处在世界的哪个位置，又为何能为自己创造出这样的空间？我要说的是，没有人会随意换工作，这根本不可能。现实情况是，你可以用这种方式来解释，但大多数人会说这是运气使然。但事实上，这是有因果关系的。如果是现在这种因果关系，你就会意识到环境对此影响巨大——如果缺乏足够的环境支持，缺乏足够的推动力，你可能会抱怨工作，但永远无法做出改变。那么有多少人说想换工作，却实际上不知道该怎么做？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So many people talk about I out of here, I've got to leave, I got to go. And then they never do. That's
turns.zh: 太多人说"我要离开这里，我必须走"，但最终却从未行动。这就是

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Right. And so what you start to realize is I have four kids and my daughter would come home one day and I'd say, how is work? And if she could name me four of the pushes, I knew she was already looking for another job. And so it's this notion of it's not anyone push, but it's when the set of pushes come together and really give you enough energy to go like, yeah, I can't see where to go. I am disrespected. And the fact is I'm not learning as much as I used to learn, I got to go find a new place. And so it's these three or four things that have to happen that ultimately cause people to say, today's the day I got to leave. But the other part is they won't leave if they don't know where to go. (00:16:30): And so a lot of people end up, they have enough energy to leave, but then they actually just go get another job in the same position they had before and that it's actually worse, the same or worse than it was the other place. And so part of this is that you have to understand what does progress mean to you? So we have to talk about the polls, which are these things that happen to you that the outcomes that you're actually seeking by going to this job. And it's not more money. Like 53% of the people who basically said they got more money, did not get more money. They told the company they had more money because they knew they couldn't argue with having them come back because they got more money. And in their mind they're like, if they give me that much money, I'll stay. And it's like it's not really the reason. And so this is where you start to peel back that onion and you realize it's very, very fertile in terms of all this energy to cause people to make a job change.
turns.zh: 对的。所以你会意识到，我有四个孩子。有一天女儿回家后问：工作怎么样？如果她能列出四条推动因素，我就知道她已经在寻找新工作了。所以关键不在于有没有推动因素，而在于当一系列推动因素汇聚在一起，真正为你注入足够能量时，你才会意识到"是的，我找不到出路了。我受到了不尊重。"事实上，我学不到以前那么多东西了，我必须去寻找新环境了。所以有三四个条件必须同时满足，最终促使人们说："今天就是我离开的日子了。"但另一方面，如果不知道去哪里，他们是不会离开的。（00:16:30）：所以很多人最终有足够的能量离开，但实际上只是在原职位上换一份工作，结果甚至更糟、和之前一样糟糕。那么关键在于，你必须理解进步对你的意义是什么？所以我们要谈谈"民意调查"，即工作带来的、你真正追寻的结果。不是更多的钱。比如53%声称涨了工资的人实际上并没有涨工资。他们告诉公司涨了工资，是因为知道无法反驳公司用涨薪来挽留人才的借口。在他们心里，"如果给我那么多钱，我就会留下。"但这其实不是真正的原因。所以这时候你需要层层剖析，就会发现这种能量在促使人们换工作方面非常有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to go back to people looking for a job right now, but before we do that, you talked about energy drivers, energy drains. This is such an important and fertile area and you have an actual guide for helping you figure out what gives you energy, what drains your energy so that you can find work that gives you energy, which is really important, share advice on how to figure this out for yourself.
turns.zh: 我想回到当前正在找工作的人群中来，但在此之前，您提到了“能量驱动因素”和“能量消耗因素”。这是一个非常重要且富有成效的领域，您甚至为此编写了一份实用指南，帮助人们识别能为自己注入能量的事物，以及会消耗自身能量的因素。这样一来，人们就能找到能为自己带来能量的工作，此举至关重要。您能否分享一些方法，帮助人们自己去探索这一点呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: One of the things we do in the book, so it's nine steps for you to basically go through. And the reality is I would tell you, I'm not sure anybody's going to do all nine steps, but the fact is this is like if you're going to do this, this is the best of the best, but if you do five of the steps, you're going to actually be way better off. So it's like I don't want to intimidate people by nine steps, but the reality is this is a really big one, which is to go back through your career and even back to college, I've taken people back to high school and basically talk about those moments where you got energy, you walked into a situation and you literally were like, "Oh my God, I got so excited about this and =why did I get excited?" (00:18:16): It's one, capturing those moments and then dissecting those moments to say, what was it about that context that gave you energy that made you excited, right? For me, it was like, oh, learning something new. I get really excited by learning new things. And so it's like, okay, and what I realized is that when I actually know something, I actually get bored with it. It actually sucks my energy because then I got to prove myself to everybody else as opposed to trying to learn something new. The other half is these energy drains, which is this aspect of the things that you go in and just suck the life out of you. And what I started to realize is everybody's got to do some work that sucks their energy. I got to do expense reports, there's just certain things I have to do, PNL, state, all these things. (00:18:58): But the reality is most people spend 95% of their time doing the work that sucks their energy so they get the 5% of the joy of the work they do. And what I realized is that if you can pull that ratio to 40% energy drive or drain or 50 50, you don't even know you're working anymore because you're just used to basically always doing the grind to get where you want to go. And so part of this is to realize that it's about reducing stress as well, but energy drivers and drains are these things that most people have, they need some help remembering. And what I've learned is that I can interview somebody about, so tell me about this last job. Tell me about one of the greatest moments you had at that job. And we have an interview guide in the middle of it, but ultimately it's about taking time to reflect on it. (00:19:44): So what I've learned is that if I let people do it over a two-week period or so, they start to remember things like I say, go for a walk and just think about that job you had back then. And they'll go like, "Oh, I remember these people. I love working with these people." All right, well, what was it about that? And so it's this reflective nature of pulling out those things that give you energy because if you're in a place that gives you energy, again, it doesn't feel like you're working. And so it's really important to find these moments of both energy drivers and energy drains to create the requirements of what you're trying to look for. Because in hindsight, the fact is those are the aspects of what almost like your DNA is wired this way.
turns.zh: 书中列出了九个步骤供大家参考。说实话，我不确定所有人都能完成全部九个步骤，但关键在于，即便只完成其中五个步骤，也能带来显著提升。所以我不想用九个步骤把大家吓到，但现实是这确实至关重要——回顾你的职业生涯，甚至追溯到大学时期。我曾带人回溯到高中阶段，探讨那些让你充满活力、一走进某个场景就忍不住感叹“天哪，我太兴奋了”的时刻。（00:18:16）关键在于捕捉这些瞬间，然后剖析背后的原因：是什么样的环境激发了你的能量，引发了这种兴奋感？对我而言，是学习新知识。每当接触新事物时，我都会格外激动。后来我发现，当我真正掌握某项技能后，反而会对它失去兴趣，因为这时我不得不向他人证明自己的能力，而非专注于探索新知。另一半是能量消耗源——那些让你精疲力竭的工作。比如做费用报表、处理PNL、州政府事务等，这些事务确实耗费精力。但现实是，大多数人95%的时间都在处理消耗能量的工作，仅获得5%的工作乐趣。我意识到，如果能将这个比例调整至40%能量驱动或消耗，或50:50，你甚至会忘记自己在工作，因为你早已习惯了为达成目标而埋头苦干。关键在于减压，但能量驱动与消耗源是大多数人需要铭记的概念。我曾采访别人：谈谈你上一份工作。回想你在那份工作中最美好的时刻。我们在访谈指南中设计了这个环节，但最终还是要静下心来反思。（00:19:44）经验表明，若给人们两周时间，他们会开始回忆。比如散步时回想当时的团队成员。他们会感慨：“哦，我还记得这些人。和他们一起工作真开心。” 追问背后的原因至关重要。身处能激发能量的环境时，工作就不再像工作了。因此，识别能量驱动与消耗源的关键意义在于，帮助你明确理想状态的要素。回首往事时，你会发现这些特质深深根植于你的基因中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In the book you have all these nine steps, all the details. You talked about how maybe give it two weeks to let it all bubble up. For folks that maybe just are listening to this and want to do a quick thought exercise at least or something in the next day to help them figure out a little bit of what gives them energy, not what do you suggest they do?
turns.zh: 书中列出了九个步骤，所有细节都写得清清楚楚。你提到或许可以给人们两周时间，让他们慢慢回想。针对那些可能只听听就想快速做个思考练习，或者想在第二天就行动的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I was coaching somebody the other day and basically they came to me and said, I really hate my job. I just really want to quit. I'm like, okay, but let me ask this. In the last 12 months, can you think of a time where you literally enjoyed the moment or two? And they're like, yeah, I have a couple of those. And you start to write them down and then you say, all right, well tell me the things that really suck your energy. And they write them down and then they think about another thing that was basically a moment, but it's about capturing these moments. And most people, they think their job is supposed to do everything for them and the reality is it's not. And so part of it's being able to help them balance that out and realize that even in a situation that you think is horrible, there's a lot of things you're learning in the middle of it and it's important to realize and understand what they are. (00:21:22): And so I would tell people just to take the time to reflect and say, think about two or three meetings, think about two or three projects, two or three things that you did where literally when you went into it, you actually had an X amount of energy and when you came out of it, you actually had 2X, 3X, four x of energy and say, what was it about that project or that meeting or that team that gave you so much energy and to be able to make it explicit. So actually that becomes a design requirement for your next job. At the same time we're going to talk about things you suck at. I always talk about strength finders and I tell people to say, I want to know the bottom five. (00:22:01): And they're like, why? It's because those are the five things you really suck at that you don't even know you suck at. And that's typically where the energy drains come from. And so it's basically having them look back and say, where are those moments where? And ultimately now dissecting, why does it suck? Does it suck because you don't know? Does it suck because you've done it a thousand times? Does it suck because it's not the right culture? What are the things that actually make it suck? So you can come up with another set of design requirements. So ultimately I'm treating you as a product to understand what are your requirements basically to be able to make progress.
turns.zh:
最近我在指导一位学员时，他跟我说自己很讨厌现在的工作，一心想辞职。我问他：“过去12个月里，你有没有哪一刻真正享受过工作？”他回答：“有过几次。”我让他把那些时刻写下来，并问：“现在回想，那些时刻里最消耗你能量的因素是什么？” 学员列举了几个例子，然后开始反思那些看似糟糕的经历背后的积极意义。

我接着说：“大多数人总觉得工作应该为他们解决一切问题，但现实并非如此。关键在于帮助他们平衡这种认知，意识到即便身处看似糟糕的境地，你也能从中收获许多宝贵的成长。”（00:21:22）我建议学员抽出时间反思：回想两三次会议、两个三项任务，记录那些投入时充满活力而结束时精力倍增的时刻。这些积极体验实际上能为未来的职业设计提供方向。

同时，我会谈到个人能力短板：“我常提到‘优势识别器’，建议学员列出自己最不擅长的五项技能。（00:22:01）”学员质疑：“为什么要看弱项？”我回答：“因为这些未被察觉的短板才是能量流失的根源。通过复盘，你能分析：是能力不足？重复次数过多？还是文化不符？这些深层原因才能转化为设计改进的路径。”  

最终，我将学员视为产品，帮助他们明确成长的核心需求，推动职业进步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That resonates. What are some examples of drains and energizers that you've come across often just for people to have a little mental model of what to think about?
turns.zh: 这番见解很深刻。能否举几个常见的能量消耗与激活的例子，方便大家建立思维框架？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So, for example, again, somebody I was coaching, they love to learn and they realize that the fact is once they learn something, it's like it becomes boring to them. And so this notion of being able to actually learn on a regular basis and have ongoing things. And so we talked, we'll talk about prototyping later, but what jobs do you actually always get new things that you have to learn? And so while consulting is one of those like, "Oh, I've never done consulting." That's interesting. Oh, you could do customer success. Well, that's not new. I'm like, every customer's different. Every customer has a different situation. You have to learn their situation. "Oh yeah, okay, I can learn that way." So part of it is being able to actually extract those things about what learning is and then being able to then translate it into what can we do with it. So learning. (00:23:31): There's one about basically helping others. So one of mine that gives me energy is what I call a maximizer or an individualizer. Like I really love to basically help people find their way. And so everybody who's ever worked with me or I've coached in my life, it is about me being able to figure out who they are and where can they go. And so this book is a natural extension of that skill that I have and that I like to do. And so it's not surprising I got here, but I never would've guessed that I would've ended up in the HR space trying to help people find the work. So drains can be everything from some people love the routine and gives them energy and other people hate the routine. It actually sucks their energy. And so you start to realize this is the part of building a team is that when I start to realize the things that drain my energy and I suck at, I should actually find my teammates that actually love to do the stuff I suck at or love the stuff that drains my energy. (00:24:28): Because ultimately that's the diversity of a team that actually makes it really work. And so instead of trying to, most people try to hire people like themselves, and that actually is where it goes wrong because then you end up with a very large blind spot where ultimately if you start to realize what you're good at, what you suck at, what gives you energy, what sucks your energy and start to really complement it with other people. So my business partner of 25 years is my exact opposite. What I love to do, he hates to do what he loves to do. I hate to do all practical purposes, we should not get along, but he's my best friend. And ultimately the fact is we trust each other enough so he knows what not to give me. And when something comes on my plate that he knows that is really hard for me to do, he'll take it off and say, let me give you a draft and you can look at this. I'm like, oh, perfect. And so these are the kinds of things you really start to think about.
turns.zh:
举个例子，我之前指导过的一个人，他们热爱学习，但意识到一旦掌握了某项技能，学习过程往往会变得乏味。因此，我们探讨了如何能够持续学习、持续成长。稍后我们会详细谈论原型设计，但先来聊聊哪些工作能让人不断接触新事物、不断学习？比如咨询行业，有些人会说：“哦，我从没做过咨询。”这很有趣。还有客户成功团队，但那又不是新领域。我会回应：“每个客户都不同，每个客户的情况各异，你必须去了解他们的处境。”对方回应：“哦，好的，我可以那样学习。”关键在于提炼出学习的本质，然后转化为实际行动。

（00:23:31）：有一种职业模式，核心是帮助他人。比如我所擅长的“最大化者”或“个性化者”，就是帮助人们找到自己的方向。与我共事过的人或我指导过的客户，都能感受到我善于发掘他们的潜力和发展方向。这本书是这种技能的自然延伸。毫不奇怪，我会走上这条路，但从未预料到自己会进入人力资源领域，帮助人们找到理想工作。

（00:24:28）：消耗能量的事物各不相同——有些人热爱日常的重复工作并从中获得能量，而另一些人则厌恶这种常规，认为它吸走了自己的精力。组建团队的关键在于，当我意识到哪些事让我精疲力竭、哪些事我做得不好，时我就应该寻找那些热爱我不擅长之事的队友，或者喜欢做让我精疲力竭之事的伙伴。

（00:25:34）：多样性是团队成功的关键。大多数人倾向于招募与自己相似的人，这恰恰是错误的策略，因为这样会形成巨大的盲区。只有当我们真正了解自己的优势与短板，清楚哪些事能激发能量、哪些事让人精疲力竭，并与团队成员形成互补时，团队才能真正运转起来。

（00:26:28）：我25年的商业伙伴与我截然相反。我热爱的事，他厌恶；我厌恶的事，他热爱。表面上我们应该合不来，但他是我最好的朋友。关键在于我们充分信任彼此——他知道哪些工作我不擅长，当我无法胜任某项任务时，他会接手并说：“我给你起个草稿，你看看。”这才是团队协作的真谛。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Many people listen to this might be like, okay, great, I'm going to find that my energizers are check Twitter all day, go to the beach. And it's like, how can I find a job that is the energizer and there's not drains and all these things?
turns.zh: 许多听众可能会想，嗯，很好，我要找到自己的能量来源，比如整天刷推特、去海边玩。但问题是，如何找到既能激发能量、又没有消耗的职业呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So this is where you have to go... This is where you have to abstract it beyond the beach. Why do you like to go to the beach? This is where you have to go. So there's three layers of language I talk about. One layer is the problem layer. I love to go to the beach. It's like, okay, but you have to understand, well, why do you love to go to the beach? Oh, I love the sun, I love the waves. I'm like, okay, but when you go to the beach, where do you get? Tell me about a day with the beach where you got energy and tell me about a day at the beach where you didn't get energy. (00:25:54): It's like, oh, and there's a lot of people around, oh, I like to be around people. So it's about abstracting it down to a level of causation so you understand what causes the beach to be a fun place. And most people just stay up at the problem layer and they don't really dig deep enough to understand what causes it to say why they like the beach. And so we talk about that in the book in terms of how do we unpack the language so you understand the causal mechanisms.
turns.zh: 所以这就是你需要去的地方……这就是你需要将其抽象化到超越海滩的层面。你为什么喜欢去海滩？这就是你必须要做的。所以我谈到的语言有三个层次。第一个层次是问题层。我喜欢去海滩。嗯，但你得理解，你为什么喜欢去海滩？哦，我喜欢阳光，喜欢海浪。我又问，嗯，但当你去海滩时，你得到了什么？给我讲讲你在海滩度过的一天，让你充满活力的，再讲讲让你没有活力的一天。（00:25:54）比如，哦，周围人很多，哦，我喜欢和人待在一起。所以这就是要将其抽象到因果关系的层面，让你理解是什么让海滩成为一个有趣的地方。大多数人只停留在问题层，而没有真正深入探究是什么导致他们喜欢海滩。所以我们在书中讨论了如何解析这种语言，让你理解其中的因果机制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another technique that I found helpful because actually this idea of figuring out what energizes you and drains you comes up often on this podcast, and it was actually really important for me when I was left my job to figure out what I wanted to do next. The technique I found really helpful is day to day pay attention after every meeting and interaction, did this energize me and did this drain me? And then you start to detect and then spend more time on the things that energize you and less time things that drain you as much as you can.
turns.zh: 我发现另一个很有用的技巧是，实际上，在这个播客中，经常会提到如何弄清楚什么能给你能量，什么会消耗你的能量。这对我来说非常重要，当我离职后，我需要确定接下来要做什么。我发现一个很有用的技巧，就是每天在每次会议和互动之后，注意这件事是给我带来了能量，还是消耗了我的能量？然后你开始留意，尽可能多地花时间在能给你能量的事情上，少花时间在消耗你能量的事情上。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That's right. And so one of the things I'm trying to teach people now is to use AI to help them with the energy drains because most people, the one thing I've learned is that I grew up as an engineer and as an engineer was like everything should be a process. But what I've learned is if I wrap a process around something I love to do, I actually ruin it. But if I wrap a process about something I really hate to do and gamify it, I can actually get through it. And so lots of times you start to realize there's these little tricks you learn along the way that help you do that. But I would say paying attention in your day-to-day life about just reflect on the day and say, where did I get energy today and where did my energy get drained? Will just help you start to articulate those things because when it comes down to it, here's the craziest part to me of... One of the crazy parts, is the job descriptions are made up. (00:27:35): They're literally just made up. And there are a list of stuff that the manager will say, all right, we want them to do this. And then they'll think of all the stuff they don't want to do and they put that in there. And so the reality is if you actually start to look at it and say like, hey, I can do these 15 things, but there's these five things that will literally take all my energy. Is there any way we can think about where I get more of the stuff I can do versus the stuff that I really suck at? And most people don't want to say it, but when they actually do it's amazing because people go like, oh yeah, I get that. Okay, we can actually give this off to somebody else. It's crazy. So this is the other part is I look at the industry and they've tried to automate the resumes, which is it's all the stuff you did. (00:28:17): It's not the stuff you want to do. And then you end up matching it to a resume or to a job description, which is like a unicorn. We're trying to find a unicorn, and then ultimately we're trying to get people to fit the job. And you start to realize that nobody fits that job perfectly and there's too many trade-offs. But if you actually reframe this and say, how do I get the job to fit the person? And you start to realize I can change the design of the job and now they love what they do, they're never going to leave. And so you start to realize it's about actually understanding how to do that, which is I think really, really powerful. And I have some companies that are starting to do that and the results are crazy, productivities through the roof, all these different crazy things.
turns.zh: 没错。所以我现在努力教给人们的一件事，就是利用人工智能来帮助他们应对精力消耗的问题，因为大多数人——我学到的一点是，我成长为一名工程师，工程师总是认为一切都应该是一个流程。但我发现，如果我用流程来规范自己喜欢做的事，反而会毁了它。但如果我把流程应用于自己讨厌做的事，并将其游戏化，就能顺利完成任务。因此，你会逐渐意识到，过程中有很多小技巧可以帮到你。但我要说，日常生活中多留意，回顾一天的经历，问问自己今天哪里获得了能量，哪里消耗了能量，这会帮助你清晰这些问题。说到根本，最让我惊讶的是……最疯狂的一点是，职位描述都是虚构的。（00:27:35）它们完全是编造出来的。经理会列出一堆想让员工做的事，然后把自己不想做的事写进去。现实情况是，如果你真正审视职位描述，发现自己能胜任其中15项，但有5项会彻底耗尽你的精力。有没有办法让工作更符合你的长处，而非你的短处？大多数人不愿承认，但一旦尝试就会惊喜发现，原来我能把这些事交给别人啊。这太神奇了。这也是我观察到的另一个现象：行业试图自动化简历筛选，但简历都是你做过的事（00:28:17），而非你想做的事。最终你会发现，没有人能完美契合某个职位标准，总是有太多权衡。但如果你转换思路，问自己如何让工作适合人而非相反，你会发现可以调整工作设计，让员工热爱自己的工作，永不离职。这才是关键所在，我认为这真的非常强大。我已有一些公司开始实践这种方法，成果令人惊叹，生产力飙升，各种奇迹频现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I definitely want to come back to that when we talk about finding and keeping awesome people. And that's a great foreshadowing of that. I wanted to double down on the importance of this discussion of finding energy drivers and drains. Because going back to the first question asked of the difference between job features and job experiences is my sense is understanding what energizes you will help you find a job, will help you overcome these features of a fancy title and a fancy salary and focus more on the experiences such that you are happier and thrive at this new job and love it versus tricked with this awesome title and salary.
turns.zh: 等我们讨论如何吸引和留住优秀人才时，我肯定会再回过头来探讨这个话题。这对那次讨论是个很好的铺垫。我想进一步强调找到能量驱动因素和消耗因素的重要性。回到最初的问题——职位特质和职位体验的区别——我的理解是，理解什么能激发你的能量，将帮助你找到工作，帮助你突破华丽头衔和高薪的表象，更多关注工作体验，这样你才能在新工作中更快乐、更高效，而不是被虚荣的头衔和薪资所迷惑。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: We to map the features to the experiences that actually make it happen because features are actually static, your job title, but if I get the title, I can impress others, I can make people think, that makes me feel like I'm making products to go from a director to a VP. Right? And so part of it's I actually understand why do you want that feature and what is it going to do for you? So it's this notion of, again, action as opposed to most features are static, so what does it actually do for you? And what happens through time is that title will wear down over time. And so it has a depreciation to it that now I've been a VP, now I got to be a C-level person. So all of a sudden you start to realize that feature, which is really important in the beginning, ends up being a push in the end because it's like, hey, I haven't gotten promoted in a while.
turns.zh: 我们的目标是将产品功能与实际实现这些功能的用户体验相匹配，因为功能本质上是静态的，比如你的职位头衔。然而，如果我获得了这个头衔，我就能给别人留下深刻印象，让人们刮目相看，这让我觉得自己在做产品时能从总监晋升到副总裁。对吧？所以关键在于，我要真正理解你为什么想要这个功能，它能为你带来什么价值？这就回到了行动导向的理念——大多数功能都是静态的，但它能为你带来什么实际好处？随着时间推移，这个头衔会逐渐失去光彩。比如，我现在是副总裁了，但接下来就得晋升到C级高管职位了。突然你会意识到，这个最初非常重要的功能，最终却成了阻碍晋升的累赘，因为你会想，嘿，我好久没升职了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then you end up being in that VP role and what this sucks, what am I doing here?
turns.zh: 当你身处副总裁职位时，又会陷入迷茫：这份工作太糟糕了，我在这里干什么？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, well, so that's the other part is you start to realize how many people look around. What are the big pushes is when I look around and I don't want my boss's job and I don't know where to go next. And the fact is, what happens is an opening comes up and they put you into a position that you don't want and then you're like, I don't really want to do this. And so ultimately a lot of this starts when they can't see where they can grow and go. And so it starts to realize, and that's where a lot of this starts. And so letting people understand what they can do and where they can go is really, really important. And again, we'll get to that, but that's a big one.
turns.zh: 是啊，所以另一个关键点是，你会意识到周围很多人都在观望。最重要的推动力是什么？当我环顾四周时，发现自己既不想接手老板的职位，又不知道下一步该往哪儿走。事实上，当空缺职位出现时，他们把你安排到一个你不想要的职位上，你就会觉得，我其实不愿意做这个。归根结底，许多问题始于人们看不到自己的成长和晋升机会。让人们明白自己能做什么、能去哪里，真的非常重要。我们稍后会详细探讨这一点，但这确实是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to somebody looking for jobs. So they either got let go, they left a job, they hid it and they haven't found some new, what are just some tactics you suggest based on this framework to help them be more successful?
turns.zh: 我想再回到求职者的话题。他们可能被裁员、主动离职、隐藏失业状态却找不到新工作。基于这个框架，你能给出哪些策略帮助他们更成功？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So the first thing I would say is when you can distill this down to the things that give you energy and what you're good at, the thing that I think has been most powerful is, again, treating you like a product. How do we prototype different job positions for you? So how do we think of you? So I was talking to somebody or I was coaching somebody who was a neuroscientist and they had just come back from Ireland and they were running this big lab and they got burnt out and they came and basically took a job at a hospital. And as she started to talk about what gave her energy and not, we said, well, what about being a design researcher? What about being a National Geographic coordinator? So it's this notion of prototyping wide because what we realize is most people don't feel like they have agency to go anywhere else. (00:32:03): And the reality is if you're really good at the things you're good at, they're used in a lot of other places. And so you'd think, boy, if I'm in finance or I'm in marketing in a financial corporation, oh I got to find another financial company. But if you're good at marketing and you like what you do, you can go to a lot of different places. And so it's this notion of starting by doing what we call informational interviews to other jobs that are out there. So it's like I was coaching somebody and I said, all we're this person that was the neuroscientist. It's like, all right, we're going to go find somebody who's in that geo coordinator, we're going to go to LinkedIn and find somebody who either had the job or has the job and you're going to interview them to say, "What's it like to have this job?" (00:32:42): And this does two things. It gives you practice talking about yourself and talking to other people, which most people haven't done in a long time. And the other part is it allows you to start to put yourself in that situation and go like, well, this really worked for me or not. And it turned out the fact is she was thinking she could travel and she could do science and she could help people be a teacher. And it turns out that geo coordinator is just like a travel agent. It literally, it's all pre-programmed and everything else. And she's like, "Oh, I'm out." And so it is helping them actually put the rubber to the road on some of these notions because most people start applying for jobs, but they really don't know what they are. And so what I would tell you is one is as somebody looking for a job is distill your skills, distill what gives you energy, distill those things and make sure you're clear on those. (00:33:32): Go wide and find what many different industries that can do it. Go talk to friends, people who have these jobs and start to realize what they are and narrow down to one area that you really feel like you can actually go to that's going to give you the outcomes that you want. It's this notion of prototyping very wide to learn and then using it to narrow and then basically figure out the real thing you want to go after and why you want to go after it.
turns.zh:
首先，我想说的是，当你能将自己的兴趣和专长提炼出来，就好像把自己当作一款产品来设计一样。这时候，我们要问自己：如何为你量身定制不同的职位原型？又该如何重新审视你的职业定位呢？我曾与一位刚从爱尔兰回国的神经科学家交流。她原本在运营大型实验室，但因工作压力过大而辞职，最终选择在医院担任职务。当我们探讨她的兴趣所在时，我们提出了诸如“设计研究员”或“国家地理杂志协调员”等可能性。这其实是在拓宽职业探索的边界，因为我们发现大多数人认为自己没有足够的主动性，无法转换到其他领域。（00:32:03）现实情况是，如果你擅长自己所长，这些技能在其他领域同样适用。你或许会想：“如果我在金融或市场营销领域工作，就只能跳槽到另一家金融公司。”但如果你热爱市场营销，完全可以转战其他行业。因此，我们建议先通过信息访谈探索不同领域的可能性。

比如，我曾指导一位神经科学家，她想转行到地理信息协调员岗位。我们首先在领英上寻找相关从业者，邀请他们分享工作体验。这不仅锻炼了她的表达能力，还让她清晰认识到自己是否适合该职位。结果发现，这个职位本质上就是旅行代理，所有流程都高度标准化。她顿时失去兴趣。可见，实践验证比空想更有价值。

因此，我建议求职者首先明确自身优势，量化能量来源，再通过广泛探索不同行业，逐步锁定目标。（00:33:32）具体步骤包括：拆解技能，提炼核心价值，开展信息访谈，确认职业定位，拓宽探索范围，最后缩小范围至心仪领域并找到动力。这种方法能帮助求职者快速验证职业方向，避免盲目申请。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how, again, this relates to a product where when you're designing the product, you've talked to potential customers of this thing and understand what problems they have and it's a fit.
turns.zh: 我特别赞同将职业探索视为产品设计的理念。就像设计产品时要深入了解用户痛点并提供解决方案一样，我们需要与潜在雇主沟通，理解他们的需求，并找到契合点。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That's right. Here's the thing is job descriptions should really be, here's the context we're in. Here's what this role is about. Here's what progress means in this role and here's how we will actually reward you for actually doing this work. And it's just not that way. And so again, I'm working on another extension of this book around just helping companies implement this. And so it's so fascinating. It's like it's a thread that just keeps pulling. I keep pulling.
turns.zh: 没错。关键在于，职位描述应该清晰传达我们所处的环境、这个职位的核心职责、职位进展的衡量标准，以及我们将如何为实际工作成果提供回报。但现实往往并非如此。因此，我正在围绕这一主题撰写一本扩展读物，旨在帮助企业实践这些理念。这实在太引人入胜了，就像一根不断延伸的线，我始终在不断探索。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of that, so let me try to describe the framework so far. And I know it's not complete in the book basically walks you through step by step, but it's essentially understand what's pushing you out of your current job. Was it those four quests? Are they pushing you or they're pulling you? I forget exactly.
turns.zh: 说到这儿，让我试着概括一下目前的框架结构。虽然书中没有完全展开，但基本思路是先理解是什么因素促使你离开现职。是那四个核心诉求吗？它们是推动还是拉扯你的力量？我有点记不清具体内容了。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: They're both. So the thing is there's got to be a push and then at some point if there's just push and there's no pull, the reality is that then you're just going to about your job. So part of it is the push actually gives you the energy to look, but you have to have the pulls on the other side to know which direction to go. Think of it as like a compass. And so these quests help you understand, am I going north, am I going south? Am I going east? Am I going west? Do I need control? Do I need alignment? Do I need to get out? Do I need to do it? Take the next step. And ultimately based on that, that's going to shape how we actually then load your strengths, your energy drivers, your energy drains as air, how are we going to aim this thing? So it's about aiming where you go next.
turns.zh: 两者兼有。关键在于必须有推动力，但如果只有推动力而没有拉扯力，最终你只会继续维持现状。因此，推动力能激发你去探索，但你必须有对应的拉扯力来指明前进方向。这就像指南针一样。这些核心诉求能帮助你判断：我该往北走？往南走？往东？往西？我需要掌控感？需要清晰的方向？需要突破现状？需要行动？迈出下一步。最终，这些判断将决定我们如何精准匹配你的优势、能量驱动因素和能量消耗因素，以及如何精准定位目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's exactly where I was going to go. So essentially it's figure out which of these things are pushing and pulling. You figure out what energizes you and drains you to come up with a checklist of here's what I want my next role to be. And then you do this prototyping where you interview people, you make a broad list of potential places and jobs and then interview them about what that life is like to see which checkboxes are checked.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这正是我的核心观点所在。关键在于分辨哪些因素是推动力，哪些是拉扯力。你需要明确哪些事物能激发你的能量，哪些会消耗你的能量，从而列出理想下一份工作的核心清单。然后通过访谈验证，广泛筛选潜在职位和公司，再通过访谈了解真实的工作场景，验证清单上的各个要素是否被满足。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yep. And ultimately the biggest thing is about the trade-offs you have to make. No job is perfect and ultimately people are looking for the thing that checks all the boxes and you start to realize nothing checks all the boxes. So what are you willing to give up to get? And so I was coaching somebody a while ago who basically was an entrepreneur and he was at one company and he had been there for five years. They had gone from basically being, I'll say nothing to basically being over a hundred million, but it wasn't small anymore. And he's like, I want to be a founder someday, so I want to take the next step. But the reality is like I think I want to go work for one more entrepreneur. And so they basically went for, he got four or five job offers he could make. He got one being an engineer somewhere and it was paying 3 50, 400. (00:36:33): And he had another job where he could actually work next to as almost like the chief of staff of a very well-known entrepreneur. And he would learn a lot. And so the question is, and it was like 200 and which one do you want? And he ended up taking the job with the entrepreneur to teach him, but he actually went in and said, I'm taking this job, I have this other job for this other money. I'm giving up this much money so I can learn from you. And he said, fine, I'll make you chief of staff. And ultimately he said, and you're here for two years so you can be a founder. So they actually reframed the job to literally fit him. And then what I told him is, you can't go back and bitch about the money because you made the trade-off to do it. (00:37:11): So you can't go like, "Oh God, I should get more money." It's like, this is how it is and this is a choice you made live with it, but put a timeframe on it. And so it's these trade-offs that are really, really important and actually landing the job because most people want it all. And I mean if you look back on your career, you never got it all. And so the other part is to realize a side gig or a hobby or these other things can actually supplement some of those other energy drivers. You get from basically the job that you can't get everything from the same job.
turns.zh: 是的。归根结底，最重要的是你必须做出权衡。没有一份工作是完美的，人们总是在寻找能满足所有条件的职位，但你最终会发现没有任何工作能完全符合所有标准。所以你愿意为了获得什么而放弃什么？不久前我指导过一个人，基本上他是一位创业者，在一家公司工作了五年。他们从几乎一无所有发展到年营收过亿，但公司规模已经不算小了。他说自己想成为创始人，所以想迈出下一步。但现实是，我觉得他应该再为另一位创业者工作一年。他收到了四五份工作邀请，其中一份是工程师职位，薪资在3.5万到4万美元之间。还有一份工作是能在一位知名创业者的幕僚长身边工作，能学到很多东西。问题是，年薪20万美元，你选哪一份？他最终选择了那位创业者的职位，但他进去后对老板说：“我接受这份工作，但我还有另一份高薪工作。为了向你学习，我愿意放弃这笔钱。”老板说：“好吧，我让你当幕僚长。”最终他说：“你在这里工作两年后，就可以去创业了。” 所以他们重新规划了职位，使其完全适合他。我告诉他，不能回头抱怨薪资，因为这是你做出的权衡选择。（00:37:11）所以你不能说：“天哪，我应该拿更高的薪资。” 现实就是如此，这是你做出的选择，必须接受，但要设定一个时间期限。这些权衡真的非常重要，实际上能帮你成功获得工作，毕竟大多数人都想兼得。但回顾职业生涯，你从未真正得到过全部。另一方面，要意识到副业或爱好也能补充你从工作中无法获得的能量驱动因素。毕竟，同一份工作无法满足你所有的需求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Does it sometimes make sense to optimize for the features, the salary, the title, or is that generally just a bad idea versus the experiences versus these energizers?
turns.zh: 有时候，专注于职位特性、薪资、头衔是否有意义？还是说相较于实际经验和这些能量驱动因素，这通常是个糟糕的选择？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: What I've realized, and this is another insight, is I can actually, and this is a bad way to look at it, but I can actually pay people less if I give them better experiences. And so ultimately I can actually do more and then I just don't count on them staying so long. And so for me, I actually pay people, I pay them fairly well, but I know they can make more money elsewhere. And ultimately I want them to be attracted to go. So if they need more money, they should go somewhere else. But if they're here to learn, that's what I want people who are here to learn. And basically the way I work it is I give them a reasonable salary and then I give them big bonuses so they can save money to go do what they want to go do. (00:38:32): So I always see this as, I don't expect anybody to be with me though. People have been with me for a long time. It's one of those things where every year we sit down and talk about what's progress mean to you and how do we actually figure it out? And ultimately, I've added some offerings to my business that I would never do, but I know that this other person who works for me wanted to actually do more coaching. And I'm like, okay, we brought in three coaching clients and basically she loved it and that gave her basically more energy. And so part of it is to make sure that I can adapt to basically keep her here and make sure that she's making progress.
turns.zh: 我意识到，还有一个深刻的见解：如果你能为员工提供更好的体验，实际上你可以给他们更低的薪资。最终，这样做能让他们更有动力投入工作，而你也不必指望他们会长久留任。对我而言，我确实给员工不错的薪酬，但我知道他们在其他地方能赚更多钱。所以我希望吸引那些有学习意愿的人。如果他们需要更多钱，就该另谋高就。但如果他们来这里是为了成长，那才是我想要的。基本上，我的做法是给他们合理的薪水，再加上丰厚的奖金，这样他们就能存钱去做想做的事。（00:38:32）所以我从不指望员工能一直留在我身边。有些人确实跟了我很久。每年我们都会坐下来讨论“进步对你们意味着什么”，然后一起探讨如何实现目标。最终，我为公司引入了许多从前想都不敢想的服务项目。比如，有位员工想多做些辅导工作，我就支持她。我们引入了三个辅导客户，她乐在其中，干劲十足。这让我意识到，必须灵活调整策略才能留住人才，确保他们能不断进步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't think there's anything controversial about that. If you're a cool company that everyone wants to work at, people will pay, will take less salary because of the experience they're going to get and the potential.
turns.zh: 我觉得这没什么争议的。如果你是一家大家都想加入的酷公司，人们自然愿意为此付出代价——因为能获得的经验和发展潜力太诱人了。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That's right. And the other problem I realized is that when you overpay people, what happens is that they actually become more and more scared that they will lose it, and then they become more and more conservative because they don't want to rock the boat and they actually don't work. They do what they're told as opposed to do what they should do. And so you start to realize that money has a very interesting impact on behavior, and I have not studied it in any great fashion. There's many people who have studied more than me, but that observation of when I overpay people, they're all about, I just don't want to not get my bonus and you better make sure that I can. And you start to realize, but they don't know what it takes to get the bonus. And so you start to realize trying to innovate when everybody's only around bonuses, I suppose, that they love to do this work. Usually when they love to do the work, they get more bonus.
turns.zh: 没错。我还意识到，当你给员工过高薪资时，他们反而会更担心，害怕失去这份钱，于是变得谨小慎微，不敢轻易冒险，最终只能按部就班完成任务，而非主动作为。这种现象说明，金钱对行为的影响非常微妙。虽然我研究得不够深入，但有许多专家对此有更深入的分析。例如，当我给员工过高薪资时，他们就会变得特别在意：“我可不想拿不到奖金，你最好确保我能拿到。” 但他们却忽视了奖金背后的条件。由此可见，当所有人都只关注奖金时，创新就难上加难了。毕竟，如果员工热爱这份工作，才能获得更丰厚的奖金。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This idea of trade-off is such an important one. I feel like that's one of the biggest, most stressful elements of job search is deciding, okay, I have these job offers. I have one job offer. Should I wait, should I not? You talked about how there's the salary, the title versus a specific like the energize. This is going to energize me, give me what I want. There's also the trade-off of this will help me in my future career. There's always this idea, if I do this, this will help me with the next step. In the next step. Is there anything more there along trade-offs that might be helpful for people to understand?
turns.zh: 这种权衡利弊的思维方式至关重要。我觉得这是求职者最头疼的难题之一：面对多个工作机会，如何抉择？是等待还是行动？你提到薪资、职位头衔与激励感的权衡。激励感能激发热情，满足内心需求。还有为未来职业发展铺路的权衡。总有这样一个核心问题：如果我选择这份工作，对下一步会有帮助吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: The only thing that I say has really been powerful is just helping people see the trade-off. They don't actually take the time to look at this job is going to be more money, but I'm going to be doing more mundane things. Do I want more money? Again, that entrepreneur was like, I can make more money so I can save money for my startup that I want to do, or I can go here and learn what I need to do. And it was agonizing. It was back and forth of how do I figure that out? And ultimately, this is the hard answer I would say is we're all adults and as adults, we don't ever get all we want and we have to learn how to make trade-offs. And what I've learned is that I turned 60 this year, and the more I actually get comfortable with making trade-offs, the fact is the more satisfied I become. (00:41:17): And so part of this is that when you think you're supposed to get it all, the fact is the less satisfied you are. And so I think just helping people frame it and be able to say it out loud helps them actually figure out which direction they want to go. And they usually have a gut feel for which they want to do. And at the same time they have a rational part that basically it's like that, hey, I'd like to do this, but I got to do this now. And you just realize people just have to make the decision that they can live with. Right.
turns.zh: 唯一真正有影响力的做法，就是帮助人们看清权衡利弊。人们往往不愿花时间审视这份工作——薪资可能更高，但意味着要做更多重复性工作。"我想要更多钱吗？"再问这位创业者，他会说："我可以赚更多钱，为想创办的公司储备资金；或者去那里学习所需技能。" 这实在令人纠结。反复权衡如何抉择，最终我得出的深刻启示是：我们都是成年人，无法事事如意，必须学会权衡取舍。今年我已60岁，越是坦然接受权衡现实，内心越是充实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to chat with Christina Gilbert, the founder of one Schema of our longtime podcast sponsors. Hi, Christina.
turns.zh: 很高兴与我们播客长期赞助商one Schema的创始人克里斯蒂娜·吉尔伯特交流。嗨，克里斯蒂娜。

turns.speaker: Christina
turns.en: Yes. Thank you for having me on, Lenny.
turns.zh: 是的。感谢邀请，莱尼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the latest with one Schema? I know you now work with some of my favorite companies like Ramp, Vanta, scale and Watershed. I heard that you just launched a new product to help product teams import CSVs from especially tricky systems like ERPs.
turns.zh: one Schema最近有何动态？我知道你现在与Ramp、Vanta、scale和Watershed等我最喜欢的公司合作。听说你们刚推出新产品，帮助产品团队从ERP等复杂系统导入CSV数据。

turns.speaker: Christina
turns.en: Yes. So we just launched OneSchema FileFeeds, which allows you to build an integration with any system in 15 minutes as long as you can export a CSV to an SFTP folder. We see our customers all the time getting stuck with hacks and workarounds and the product teams that we work with don't have to turn down prospects because their systems are too hard to integrate with. We allow our customers to offer thousands of integrations without involving their engineering team at all.
turns.zh: 是的。我们刚刚推出了OneSchema FileFeeds，只要能将CSV导出到SFTP文件夹，15分钟内就能与任何系统集成。我们发现客户常被集成难题困扰，而我们的客户无需因系统集成难题拒绝潜在客户。我们让客户无需动用工程团队，即可提供数千种集成服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can tell you that if my team had to build integrations like this, how nice would it be to be able to take this off my roadmap and instead use something like OneSchema and not just to build it, but also to maintain it forever.
turns.zh: 我可以想象，如果我的团队要自己开发这类集成功能，能将其移出路线图，改用OneSchema该多好——既能快速集成，又能长期维护。

turns.speaker: Christina
turns.en: Absolutely, Lenny. We've heard so many horror stories of multi-day outages from even just a handful of ad records. We are laser-focused on integration reliability to help teams end all of those distractions that come up with integrations. We have a built-in validation layer that stops any bad data from entering your system, and one Schema will notify your team immediately of any data that looks incorrect.
turns.zh: 确实如此，莱尼。我们听过太多因为少数广告记录出错导致多日服务中断的恐怖故事。我们专注于集成可靠性，帮助团队消除集成带来的干扰。我们内置验证层，阻止错误数据进入系统，一旦发现异常数据，OneSchema会立即通知团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that importing incorrect data can cause all kinds of pain for your customers and quickly lose their trust. Christina, thank you for joining us. And if you want to learn more head on over to oneschema.co, that's oneschema.co. So you said you interviewed a thousand people over the 15, over 15 years to develop this book and this approach. When people make trade-offs, is there just a heuristic of this is what usually ends up leading you to be happiest?
turns.zh:
我知道导入错误数据可能会给客户带来诸多困扰，并迅速失去他们的信任。克里斯蒂娜，感谢你加入我们。如果你想了解更多信息，请访问oneschema.co，网址是oneschema.co。  
你提到为了写这本书和开发这种方法，你在15年间采访了1000人。当人们做出权衡时，是否存在一种启发式方法，即最终能让他们最为满意的选择？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: It depends on the quest you're in. So for example, if it's a get-out situation, it's like I actually need to go find a, so I call it a jobcation, which is a job I can go do with one hand tie by high my back so I can rest and recover to go do something else. And so you start to realize there's these different... There's a side step to build some skills and do some other things. And so you start to realize it really depends on the quest they're on that actually then dictates what are the things that they need to do. And again, the average person stays at a job four years. (00:44:03): And so you have to realize it's not like at least our parents were... At least my parents, my parents had worked for one company their entire life. And so you start to realize this is now a skill that we have to learn how to do. And let's be clear, nobody's helping you navigate this, but if you think HR is there to help you navigate this, I would tell you that they're not. Their job is to manage risk and to fill seats. And so I always say if legal and finance had a baby, it would be HR. That's not true for all of them. But the fact is that that's how most of them come to be is because there's a lot of paperwork and it's about basically making sure you know how to treat people fairly and to make sure that you're doing, but most of the time when you go to HR to complain, they're just taking notes.
turns.zh: 这取决于你所处的阶段。例如，如果你需要脱身困境，我称之为"工作度假"——即找到一份可以单手操作、背靠靠背椅就能完成的工作，这样既能休息恢复，又能做些其他事情。于是你会意识到，人生旅程中的不同阶段，决定了你需要采取的不同策略。平均而言，人们在一份工作中待四年。（00:44:03）事实上，至少我们的父母……至少我的父母，一生都为同一家公司工作。如今，人们需要学会应对这种复杂局面。但说实话，没有人会帮你规划这条路径。如果你以为人力资源部门能帮你，那我要告诉你，他们并非如此。他们的职责是管控风险和填补职位空缺。所以我常说，如果法律和财务部门生个孩子，那就是人力资源部。虽然并非所有部门都如此，但现实是大多数人力资源部门的诞生源于繁琐的文书工作，其核心职责是确保公平对待员工和合规操作。然而当你向人力资源部门投诉时，他们往往只是在记录问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is jobcation concept. I love that you touched on, I was going to ask about it. The idea of a jobcation is what it sounds like. It's a job where it's less demanding, gives you a chance to recuperate for the next step.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你提到的"工作度假"概念。正如你所说，它的本质正如其名——一份压力较小、能让你休整以迎接下一步挑战的工作。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: My jobcation was, is I had done three startups and then I started a small private equity firm around 2000. I ended up raising some money, but the fact is the internet bubble burst, and so it was about buying things for 10 cents on the dollar and selling them for 20 cents on the dollar. I hated it. I absolutely hated it. And I was traveling all over the world doing all these different things, but it was just so demanding and my family suffered. And so it got to the point of like, okay, I need to go find a job where I can actually just stay at home. I had four kids and I need to rebuild the relationship with my family. And so my jobcation was to go to build houses, and so I became a VP of sales and marketing with the intention to buy in as an owner. (00:45:47): But the fact that I wanted to work there for a year, I ended up working there for four years. I could be home every night for dinner. I lost all my status on the airlines. I literally was able to rebuild my relationship with my family. It was amazing. But it was literally a jobcation because the industry was, so, I was applying all these very advanced concepts to building homes and we grew from a hundred homes to 400 homes in three years. And so it was this aspect of it. It was a lot of fun, but it was like I was able to do a jobcation around that.
turns.zh: 我的工作度假经历是，2000年左右，我创办了三家初创公司，随后成立了一家小型私募股权公司。虽然成功筹集了资金，但互联网泡沫破裂后，我们只能以1美元购买10美元资产，再以2美元出售。我痛恨那段经历。每次出差全球各地做各种事情，都让我精疲力竭，家庭也深受其害。最终我决定找一份能让我在家陪伴孩子的工作。那时我有四个孩子，急需重建与家人的关系。于是我选择去建房子，担任销售和市场副总裁，目标是成为股东。（00:45:47）但原本计划工作一年却延续了四年。每晚我都能回家共进晚餐，但航空里程数清零了。我成功重建了与家人的关系，感觉棒极了。但这确实是一次工作度假，因为整个行业都需要我将先进理念应用于房屋建设，我们在三年内从100套房扩展到400套。这就是其独特之处——既充满乐趣，又能实现工作与生活的平衡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like a lot of people listening are like, I could use a jobcation.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多听众会想：“我也想来一场‘工作度假’。”

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, but, and this is where people go like, "Oh, I should be a director." It's like, you know what? If you're exhausted, sometimes you just put a time limit on it and say, I'm going to go do this job. And by the way, they're so appreciative to have you because you're literally working in a place where you're probably one of the smarter ones or you're one of the more experienced ones. And the reality is like they'll do a lot more than you think. And so they were so happy to have me as part of this organization and I learned a lot and I was able to rebuild my... I was very thankful for that opportunity in my life. But there was a point where I was like, yeah, okay, I'm rested, ready to go. Got to move on.
turns.zh: 是啊，但这时候人们就会说：“哦，我应该去当导演。”但你知道吗？如果你已经精疲力竭，有时候就给自己设定一个期限，说：“我要去干这份工作了。” 顺便说一句，他们很感激你的加入，因为你所在的环境里，很可能你是更聪明或更有经验的人之一。而现实是，他们能做的远超你的想象。所以他们很高兴我能加入这个组织，我学到了很多，也得以重建自己的……我非常感激人生中那段机会。但当时我也想，嗯，好吧，我休息好了，准备继续前进了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just don't tell them you're calling it a jobcation.
turns.zh: 别告诉他们你称之为“工作度假”。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I've actually told people, I've talked to somebody who just got out of a startup and just say, I need a jobcation. Here's what that means to me. Are you willing to hire me? They're like, "Yes." Because they know they don't have to pay them the full salary. They're paying. It's not about money. It's about actually being able to go to the gym and work out and have some vacations and just almost... I am a big proponent that when you're in a startup, it changes who you are. And the moment that you get out of that environment, you need to take the time to reset your mind and your body back to who you really are. Because at some point it's not you. It's the combination of the context you're in. (00:47:40): And so once you pull you from the context, I tell people, especially people who have exited a company, I tell them, you got to take a year off and you got to actually get comfortable doing nothing because the moment you are comfortable doing nothing, you know who you are again. And you can actually figure this out if you just tried to go start something right after you did the other. It's just like you think everything's easy and it's not.
turns.zh: 实际上我跟人说过，我和刚从初创公司出来的人聊天，直接说：“我需要一次‘工作度假’。” 这对我来说意味着什么？你愿意雇用我吗？他们说：“愿意。” 因为他们知道不必支付全额薪水。他们愿意出钱。这不是钱的问题，而是能去健身房锻炼、度假、放松……我非常赞同在初创公司工作会改变你的人性。一旦离开那个环境，你就需要花时间让身心回归到真实的自己。因为在某个阶段，那不是你，而是环境的组合。（00:47:40）所以一旦脱离那个环境，我告诉人们，尤其是那些离职的人，你得休息一年，真正适应无所事事的感觉。因为当你能自在地无所事事时，你才能再次认清自己。如果你刚离职就急着创业，就会发现一切并非易事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. What I love is you have... So far, you had... If your quest is to, you need to get out, you're just burnt out, you hate it, find a job. I love how simple that heuristic is. Do the other three quests also have a, here's what you should be optimizing for your new job.
turns.zh: 好的。我喜欢的是你有……到目前为止，你有……如果你想离开，精疲力竭，厌倦了现状，那就找份新工作。我喜欢这种简单的方法论。另外三个任务是否也有对应的优化建议，适合新工作呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I don't know if they're that simple, but I think that the notion of the next step is to make sure it's a big enough step. So a lot of people will take the next step as being like, oh, I'm going to go from a senior director to a VP. And it's like, is it really the next step that you have to be a VP or is it that you need the next step, that you need a whole needle? You need to go from sales to marketing. And so part of it is helping you to redefine what that step is. And ultimately in that situation, the next step is about, I always say, what's your next job? Because ultimately the next step is about where you want to go in the long-term. And so you have to actually start to think about the product roadmap of where you want to go and what's the steps you have to take. Right? (00:49:01): Control is really about basically being able to simplify the job and realize what you're really good at. And just so I think Kim Scott talks about rising stars and rock stars. I think when it's about regaining control, this is about you're a rock star. How do you get back to doing what you're really good at? You're a rock and role player and they got you playing classical music. It's like, okay, I can read the music I do that. Let me get back to rock and roll and alignment. Alignment is... I'm sorry, that was alignment. Control is really about time. It's about basically being able to have the balance. (00:49:35): And a lot of people will end up saying, I just don't have control of my time. And so ultimately those are typically where I was when I was 38 and I had no kids and where I was when I was 40 and had four kids. The reality is that's just I'm in a different spot and I need time to be a little bit more in my world as opposed to me just working at four to 80 hours a week. And so ultimately that's one of the reasons why I left.
turns.zh:
我不知道他们是否真有那么简单，但我认为下一步的关键在于确保这个步骤足够重大。很多人会把下一步看作是从高级总监晋升到副总裁。但问题是，副总裁真的就是下一步吗？还是说你需要更重大的突破，比如从销售转向市场营销？所以部分工作在于帮助你重新定义下一步的含义。最终而言，在这种情况下，下一步的核心在于——我常说——你的下一份工作会是什么？因为下一步关乎你长远的职业方向。因此，你必须开始思考未来产品路线图，明确你必须迈出的关键步骤。是吧？（00:49:01）：所谓“控制力”，实质上就是简化工作职责，发现自己真正擅长之处。我记得金·斯科特曾谈到“明日之星”和“巨星”。当谈到重获控制权时，你其实就是巨星。你该如何回归擅长之道？你本是摇滚乐手，却被迫演奏古典乐曲。这时你会说，好吧，我能读懂乐谱，我来做这个。但我要回归摇滚乐，回归初心与使命的对齐。所谓“对齐”，抱歉，我刚刚说的是“对齐”。而“控制力”本质上关乎时间，就是要平衡好工作与生活的关系。
（00:49:35）：很多人最后会说：我根本无法掌控自己的时间。以我个人经历为例，38岁时我没有孩子，40岁时有四个孩子。现实是，我当时处境不同，需要时间专注自身，而非每周工作四十到八十小时。这也是我离职的原因之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, just what you covered there is so good. This is the goal of the book in my opinion so far. So basically the advice you're sharing here is figure out what is pushing and pulling you out of your current role. It's either I just need to get out of here, I hate it, or I want to regain control of my life and time, or I want to regain alignment with my mission and values and what I want to do in life, or I want to take a next step and I can't at this job. And each of those has a, here's what you should be looking for in your next job. So let me just summarize what you shared. (00:50:36): So if you find your pull and pushes, I need to get out of here, which you should be looking for, is jobcation essentially. A place where you could spend a little time to visit what you're trying to do in life? Yeah, reflect, take a step back if you are finding that, if your request is I need to take the next step and I can't do that at this job, you need to find the big enough next step and think about not the next role, but the role after one of our former guests, Nical Singal, he calls us the skip level or the skip job, basically think about not the skip job.
turns.zh:
哇，你刚刚分享的内容太棒了。在我看来，本书的核心理念就体现在此。所以你分享的建议核心在于，找出推动和拉扯你离开当前角色的力量。可能是“我必须离开这里，我讨厌这份工作”，或者“我想重获对生活和时间的控制权”，又或者“我想与使命、价值观和人生目标重新对齐”，或者“我想迈出下一步，但这份工作不允许”。每种情况下，下一份工作的核心要素都是不同的。让我总结一下你的观点。
（00:50:36）：所以如果你找到了推动和拉扯你的力量，比如“我必须离开这里”，那你应该寻找的应该是jobcation，即能让你抽出时间探索人生目标的地方？是的。如果你发现自己请求“我想迈出下一步，但这份工作不允许”，那你需要找到足够重大的下一步，思考的重点不应是下一份角色，而是继任者提到的跳级角色，或者Nical Singal所说的跳级工作。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. It's the half step. What's the half step you're going to take for the full step? Step is like, all right, but I got to make sure it's big enough that I can get to the next level. I want to be a CEO. It's like, okay, so you've got to take the next step here.
turns.zh: 对，确实如此。这是半步行动。迈出大步之前的半步是什么？比如，好的步骤，但我必须确保它足够大，以便能晋升到下一级。我想成为CEO。但问题是，好的步骤是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. And then the final quest is you want to get back into alignment with what you want to accomplish in your life and your values and all that. And so what you want to focus on there is simplifying and understanding what you're good at and then just finding a job that lets you do the thing you're great at and energizing you.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。最后一个任务是，让你重新与自己的人生目标、价值观等保持一致。所以你需要专注于简化和了解自己的专长，然后找到一份能让你发挥所长并充满活力的工作。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: And lets you do what you're good at all the time. When you're doing work that you're really good at and you love to do and it gives you energy, it's proven, the stress levels of everybody goes down and you start to realize the realignment part is really, really important because sometimes you want... You're willing to take it on because you care about people, but it's really not something you like to do, but you have to realize it has a tax on you and it has an implication of how you feel. And sometimes you'll feel stuck that you can't get out of it because well then who's going to do it? But the reality is at some point it's destroying you at the same time.
turns.zh: 并能一直做自己擅长的事。当你从事自己擅长且热爱的工作时，它能为你注入能量，事实证明，这样做能显著降低压力水平。你会意识到，重新校准方向至关重要，因为有时你愿意承担某些职责，是出于对他人的关怀，但这其实并非你所热爱之事，而你必须意识到这会消耗你的精力，并影响你的情绪。有时你会陷入困境，觉得自己无法摆脱某些职责，但现实是，到了某个阶段，这种情况会同时摧毁你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So once you have this figured out, here's what I want to index towards in the next role, this prototyping step comes in, which is figure out potential jobs that meet these requirements and go interview people that are doing those job and see if they match the checkboxes you have of what these.
turns.zh: 好的。所以一旦你想清楚了这些，下一步就是原型设计阶段——找出符合这些要求的潜在职位，然后去面试从事这些工作的人，看看他们是否符合你的要求。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That's right. And then pick one of those jobs and say, all right, I'm going to double down on that. And then how do I write a resume that actually talks about this? How do I actually talk about the skills that I have, how I can do the job as opposed to don't tell me where you were, tell me what you can do. And so you start to talk about the different aspects of the work you want to do. And so when you go into, so the first thing is when you go to interview, you actually have now done 10 to 15 interviews with informational interviews with complete strangers that make you way more comfortable with doing interviews about a job. And so you start to realize, it doesn't take too many interviews for people to realize, you know what you want, you know where you are, you know who you are, you know what you suck at. And to be honest, I've had people go like, yeah, I applied for this job and they came back with a better job for me. (00:53:20): And so part of it is this notion is they're used to everybody trying to tell them that they can do everything in that job. But when you walk in with honesty about what it is, people are just so blown back by it, you know who you are. They're almost like, wow, more about yourself than I know about myself. So the way I talk about this is a class on yourself. And so I do this for kids coming out of college and they're like, I wish I had this class in college so I would've figured out how to pick the right major for myself because I didn't end up doing that. I end up where I think I could make money or where I could do this. And you realize, but I don't like any of those things. I'm like, well, where did you find energy? And we are able to shape it, but I believe this can become a college course as well.
turns.zh: 没错。然后选定其中一个职位，坚定地投入其中。接下来如何写一份真正能传达这些信息的简历？如何突出自己的技能，说明自己能胜任这份工作——而不是一味罗列过往经历。这样你就能开始谈论自己想做工作的不同方面。面试时，由于你已经进行了10到15次信息性面试，面对完全陌生的人，你会更加从容应对。这时人们会意识到，你清楚自己的目标、现状、性格特质，以及自己不擅长的地方。说实话，我曾遇到有人说，嗯，我申请了这份工作，结果他们给我推荐了更好的工作。（00:53:20）所以关键在于，人们习惯被告知自己能胜任所有工作。但当你坦诚地说出自己的真实情况时，人们会被你的真诚所震撼。他们会惊叹，你对自己的了解比我还多。所以我把这部分内容称为自我认知课程。我为刚毕业的学生讲授这门课，他们会说，真希望大学时能学到这门课，这样就能选对专业了。而我当年却没有做到，后来才发现自己其实更擅长赚钱或做某些事。但最终发现，这些都不是我真正热爱的。所以我会问，你从哪里获得能量？我们可以塑造这种能量，但我相信这也能成为大学课程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. And what I love is you could be thinking, why am I spending 15, 20, 30, 40 hours preparing for this interview? But in reality, you're doing it to first figure out what you want to do and where you want to work. And then that happens to also be really helpful in the interview.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。我最欣赏的是，你可能会想，为什么要花15、20、30、40个小时准备面试？但实际上，你这样做是为了先弄清楚自己想做什么、想在哪里工作。然后这些准备工作也会在面试中发挥作用。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That's right. That's right. So here's the thing is I say it's answering two what I call our easy question or easy questions, but very hard answers. Who are you and who are you not? And then ultimately, what do you want? And most people just don't think about that. They're like, how do I get the next job? And so this is why I feel like everybody, the transactional level of resumes and job descriptions and interviews, and I talk to people like, yeah, I put out a hundred resumes today. I'm like, what? And you just start to realize the system, they've automated the insanity as opposed to trying to make the process better. (00:54:55): And so I'm just coming at it from a really different perspective, and like I said, this isn't for everybody, but the reality is this is one of those things where you need to take responsibility for your career and where you want to go. And this is on you. And so the reality is you can let somebody else do it and you can try to morph yourself to fit other people. But I will tell you, you will be way better off if you spend the time to figure out who you are and find a job that matches who you are.
turns.zh: 没错。没错。关键在于，我觉得这是在回答两个看似简单、实则难答的问题：你是谁，又不是谁？最终，你想要什么？大多数人却从不深思这些。他们只会想：“我怎样才能找到下一份工作？”这就是为什么我觉得大家都深陷简历、职位描述和面试的交易层面。我跟别人聊天时会说，“你今天投了一百份简历？！”他们通常会回应：“什么？！” 但你会逐渐意识到，这个系统本质上是在自动化地制造疯狂，而不是在努力优化流程。（00:54:55）所以我从一个完全不同的视角来看待这个问题，就像我说的，这套方法并非适合所有人，但现实是，你需要为自己的职业生涯负责，明确自己的方向。这责任在你自己。如果你让别人替你做决定，试图迎合他人要求，那只会适得其反。但我要告诉你，如果你花时间去探索自我，找到与自身契合的工作，那你会收获更多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a very tactical piece of advice in your book along these lines, which is how to get through the filters of applications, software, I forget how you framed it, but just advice for breaking through these filters that hiring managers have.
turns.zh: 你的书里有条很实用的建议，讲如何突破申请、软件等过滤机制。我忘了具体表述，但核心是给出突破这些招聘经理筛选机制的建议。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah. My thing is that most real jobs don't come through those filters. I can tell you as much as people say they're hiring. The fact is that the ability to get a job through that thing is part of it is just starting to tell people what you're looking for, who you are and what you're about to start telling people. And you start to realize that network effect works way better here than trying to do the regular resumes. The other part is to realize when you find a job you want, you interview people who have those jobs and you say what was on your resume? And you can figure out what to say on it because at some point, it's almost like a set of bad filters that you need to be able to get through to get onto it. And the reality is, at some point I was applying for to be on a public board and they basically, and I had somebody rewrite my resume because I can't really do that and so I had somebody help me do it. (00:56:17): And they had business leader seven times on my resume or my CV or whatever it was. And I'm like, okay, I just don't refer to myself as a business leader. And they're like, well, if it's not there seven times, you can't get through the filter. I'm like, "What?" They're like, "Really?" I'm like, "Yep, that's how this thing works." I'm like, "Wow." And so the resume writers know how all this works and they know how to, they're the people who know how to hack the system. And if you don't have a resume writer, I would strongly suggest you find one because they know which ones work and don't work and who has what filters it. Almost like it's a side gig. It's crazy.
turns.zh: 是啊。但大多数真正的工作机会并不会通过这些过滤机制。我可以告诉你，尽管很多人声称在招聘，但事实上，通过这些过滤机制找到工作的能力，本质上在于向人们传达你的需求、你的特质和你的追求。当你开始这样做时，就会意识到人脉效应在这里比常规简历更管用。另一个关键点是，当你找到心仪的工作后，去面试那些做同样工作的人时，他们会问：“你的简历上怎么写的？”而你会发现需要调整简历内容，因为某些时候，这些过滤机制简直就是一套糟糕的筛选标准，而你必须突破这些标准才能脱颖而出。现实中，我曾申请加入一家上市公司董事会，但他们要求简历里七次提到“商业领袖”这个头衔。我当时想：“好吧，我根本不自称商业领袖。”他们说：“如果你不写七次，就过不了筛选。”我说：“什么？！”他们说：“真的吗？”我说：“是啊，这就是规则。”我说：“哇。”所以，简历撰写者深谙其道，他们知道如何破解这些机制。如果你没有简历撰写者，我强烈建议你找一个，因为他们清楚哪些简历有效，哪些无效，哪些公司用了什么样的筛选机制。这简直就是副业。太疯狂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A resume writer. So they're basically professional coaches on helping you craft your resume. Is that correct?
turns.zh: 简历撰写者。所以他们本质上是帮助你打造简历的专业教练。对吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So it can get through the filters to be seen.
turns.zh: 这样才能突破筛选机制，被注意到。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. How do you find one of these?
turns.zh: 哇。那怎么才能找到这样的撰写者呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta

turns.en: And to be honest, I realized the very shorthand of my story is I help make the abstract concrete. And as long as I'm doing that in my life, I'm doing what my purpose is. turns.zh: 说实话，我意识到我故事的精髓在于将抽象概念具体化。只要我在生活中做到了这一点，我就实现了自己的使命。比如，我教孩子们冰球时，我会教他们规则：什么是越位？如何进行面板对决？如何滑冰。但谈到输赢时，我会说："有更厉害的人。"我真正致力于帮助人们实现目标。比如，当有人想换工作时，我会问："你需要做什么？"这就是为什么这属于我的专长领域。刚开始时我对这个领域毫无头绪，只能深入研究。但现在我总结出了一套具体的流程，帮助数千人成功换工作，过上更好的生活。这对每个人都适用。我知道这一点。但关键是，我们采访了各种各样的人——从奇波雷快餐店转到麦当劳，从律师转为法官。通过对大量不同人群的观察，我们总结出了一套通用的方法论，指导人们如何应对这个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 让我最感兴趣的，就是你职业生涯的这个故事。它就像是一段旅程，过程中你会遇到一些挑战，但最终你意识到并改变了一切。正因如此，虽然我可能没有那么戏剧化的情节，但我觉得你所描述的这个过程——找到能激发你热情的事物，明确自己想去的地方和目标——这些正是你故事中不可或缺的元素。而这也正是我想加入这里的原因。

(01:03:34): My business partner is great at harmony, he actually hates conflict, but the fact is he and I can have conflict and the reality is we're all better off, but he's the one who actually keeps everybody in the company really harmonized. turns.speaker: Bob Moesta

And that time off, I helped you become you again and what you're really good at. And so that's the whole thing is most people sometimes they just need to take a jobcation.

(01:07:25): And then you let them go. And the reality is what you probably want to do is actually find a way to get that person in and figure out how to actually reshape the job to fit that person. And you start to realize that's really the key to think about it. And what I would tell you is the other thing is to think about writing the job description as a set of experiences that people can have. It's almost like you need to think of the job though. I know that there's a legal part of all this. You got to think about marketing to people who want to do this. And so my whole thing is most people wait for people to raise their hand.
