(01:08:56): So there's a lot of different ways where this can be put in, but let's be clear, I wrote this, we wrote this, Michael Horn and Ethan Bernstein and I, we wrote this with the intent of helping employees hire companies. turns.zh:
真奇怪，我现在居然在用这本书来……如果你想申请我的职位，我们得按照流程来操作。基本上来说，他们得来找我，告诉我他们的能量驱动因素和消耗因素。他们得告诉我自己擅长什么，又不擅长什么。他们还得能向我详细描述过去几份工作的经历。从招聘者的角度出发，你会意识到，招聘描述往往是虚构的，关键在于要根据合适的人来调整职位，而不是让合适的人去适应职位。就像你知道的，在初创公司里，好的人才至关重要。当你找到优秀的人才时，他们看似合适，但并非完美无缺。（01:07:25）于是你就放他们走了。但实际上，或许你更应该想办法让他们加入公司，然后调整职位以适应他们。你会意识到，这才是关键所在。我想说，另一件要做的事就是把招聘描述写成人们能够体验到的一系列经历。不过你得考虑到法律层面的限制，还要针对那些想从事这份工作的人进行营销。我的核心观点是，大多数人都在等别人主动来应聘，而这些人往往已经离职了。我相信，如果你能抛开传统的招聘思路，写出这样的职位描述：嘿，快来学习这些技能，加入这样的团队——帮助他们理解工作的意义——那么会有很多人愿意尝试新职位。
（01:08:12）我认为关键在于两个方面：优化招聘描述和建立一个流程，帮助识别人们的能量驱动因素和消耗因素。比如，当有人被问到“你擅长什么？”时，他们可能会说“我工作太拼了”。但这只是个表象。我认为真正的问题是，人们往往没有深入思考自己真正不擅长的地方，因为每个人都有短板，而招聘者往往没有做好充分准备。所以那些读过这本书的招聘者会利用这些概念，比如用“推拉理论”来开启面试对话。
（01:08:56）当然，具体应用方式多种多样。但要明确一点，这本书是我和迈克尔·霍恩、伊桑·伯恩斯坦共同撰写的，目的是帮助企业招聘优秀人才。如今很多公司反馈说，我们帮助他们优化了招聘流程、职位描述和绩效评估体系。最终，公司和员工的成长必须同步，否则人才会流失。所以关键在于，要把书中的理念应用到实际管理中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So say someone's hiring right now, they have a job description. What's something they can do to improve the odds of finding someone awesome?
turns.zh: 那么假设现在有人正在招聘，他们已经有了职位描述。为了提高找到优秀人才的概率，他们可以采取哪些措施？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah. So the first thing I would do is I would actually look at the job description and unpack what you mean by things. Get it down to what are the... So, for example, they'll say five years experience. What I will tell you is that's one of the worst statements you can put on any job like recruiting thing because why five years? What is it about? What this to me is a sign that you're lazy because you're saying, oh, you need to have five years experience. For an entry entry-level job, how does that work? What do you really need to know? And so my thing is, what does somebody who has five-year experience have and be more specific about what it is so you can actually understand because there might be somebody with three years experience who's perfect, but they're not even going to apply because you put five years on there. (01:10:21): And so there's all these kinds of things. So look at the way you've written the job description, look at the way you've wrote the requirements and be more specific. It's like, yeah, you need to know Excel, PowerPoint and word, why? What do you do with it? Tell me what I'm going to do with those. Don't tell me I need the skills in that. Tell me you're going to need to be able to build PowerPoints and do things around this, which means you need to know these things. Tell them what they're going to do as opposed to what it is.
turns.zh:
是的。所以我首先要做的是仔细阅读职位描述，深入理解招聘方所说的各项要求。比如，他们会写“五年工作经验”。我要告诉你的是，这种笼统的要求在招聘中是最糟糕的，因为“五年经验”到底指什么？这背后的逻辑是什么？在我看来，这恰恰暴露了招聘方的懒惰思维——他们说需要五年经验，但对于初级职位而言，这根本不合理。真正需要什么技能呢？所以我的建议是，要明确说明五年经验的具体含义，让求职者能真正理解其中的要求。可能有三年经验的人比五年经验者更合适，但就因为你写了“五年经验”，他们甚至都不会申请。

（01:10:21）类似这样的问题还有很多。比如职位描述中写“需要熟练使用Excel、PowerPoint和Word”，但为什么要这些技能？具体应用场景是什么？别只说需要这些技能，而要说明这些工具在实际工作中的应用场景。比如你需要制作PPT、处理数据，这才是关键所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Experiences. Essentially going back to the very first question.
turns.zh: 经验问题。本质上要回归到最初的问题。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Experiences. Back to experiences and features like you're asking for features of people, five years experience, you've got an MBA. Those are all features of people. Talk about the experiences you want people to have to come into your company. This is what happens when you're an outsider looking at an industry that's just... At some point, it makes very little sense to me, right? The HR department, it is very unknown to me. I could never get a job. So this is the funny part as people ask me, when did you want to be an entrepreneur? I said, the moment that I couldn't get a job because as a dyslexic you couldn't even write a resume that anybody could see.
turns.zh: 经验问题。回到经验和技能要求。比如你要求五年工作经验、MBA学位，这些都是对求职者的要求。关键是，要清晰说明你希望应聘者具备哪些经验和能力。这就是局外人看行业的视角。某种程度上，我对招聘流程完全不理解。人力资源部门对我来说太神秘了，我自己根本找不到工作。有趣的是，当人们问我“你什么时候想创业的？” 我回答：“当我找不到工作的时候。” 因为我有阅读障碍，甚至连简历都写不清楚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For people that didn't listen to the last episode and learn that you're actually super dyslexic and can't really read or write talk, what's the extent of that for people to understand?
turns.zh: 对于没听过我上一期节目的人——我其实有严重的阅读障碍，根本写不出清晰的简历——能否详细说明一下？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: What I believe is that I had three close-head brain injuries before I was seven years old. My belief is some of it was there beforehand, some of it wasn't. But the reality is I blame it on my stupid things I did as a kid. But the reality is by the time I was 18 years old, I had a third grade reading level. I have ADHD, I am very neuro typical. And ultimately... But it turned out that the only way my mom taught me how I learned and she literally, for example, she'd have me circle the five largest words in a paragraph. I could see words that were seven letters or longer and then she'd have me guess why those five words would be together. And that's how I learned how to read. But I could memorize the five words from the first paragraph to the last paragraph, and so I could turn through a book and very quickly get a very good understanding of what the book was about, but I can't read it like everybody else reads it in terms of small words and everything else. (01:12:37): But ultimately what that did is that disability created super ability in me, which is questions. I know how to ask so many questions because that's the way I learn. And so at some point in time, my disability has caused me to have super abilities. That's why I think your weaknesses actually create your super abilities and knowing what they are is so important. And so this is where I think a lot of this comes from is to realize I was supposed to be a baggage handler or a construction worker. (01:13:03): And my mom basically told me is like, if you understand how you learn and what you do, you can do it, but you have to be careful because if you get labeled as dyslexic, you will be basically seen as special needs. And this is 19, when I got first labeled, I was put into special needs classes, which was a room at the end of the hall. You just sat in all day and didn't really learn anything because there was no real programs for any of it. So she taught me how to really school and learn my own way. And that's where I think I built my superpowers.
turns.zh:
我认为自己在七岁前曾有过三次闭合性脑损伤。我的看法是，有些问题源于童年时期的愚蠢行为，但现实是，我把这些归咎于自己幼时的错误行为。然而事实是，18岁时，我的阅读水平仅停留在三年级。我患有多动症，但在很多方面都表现得很正常。最终……但结果发现，我母亲教我的学习方法才是关键。比如，她会让我圈出段落中最长的五个单词。我能识别出七个字母及以上的长词，然后她会让我猜测这五个词为何组合在一起。就这样，我学会了阅读。但我能记住从第一段到最后一段的所有五个单词，因此我能快速通读一本书，准确理解其内容，但我无法像其他人那样流畅地阅读短句。（01:12:37）但最终，残疾赋予了我超能力——提问能力。我知道如何提问，因为这是我的学习方式。因此，在某种程度上，我的残疾反倒造就了我的超能力。这就是为什么我认为你的弱点实际上能转化为你的超能力，而认识到这一点至关重要。这也让我意识到，自己本该成为一名行李搬运工或建筑工人。
（01:13:03）我妈妈曾告诉我，如果你理解自己的学习方式和行为模式，你就能克服困难。但你必须小心谨慎，因为如果被贴上“阅读障碍”的标签，就会被视为有特殊需求。19岁时，我首次被贴上这个标签后，被安排进特殊教育班——位于走廊尽头的一间教室。在那里坐一整天却什么也学不到，因为根本没有针对这种情况的有效教学方案。所以她教会了我如何自主学习，最终培养了我的超能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I feel like I could do a whole episode deep dive into this. I just had Tobias Lütke on the podcast, the CEO of Shopify, he's also dyslexic. And we actually didn't get that.
turns.zh: 哇。我觉得我可以专门做一期深入探讨这个话题的播客。我最近刚邀请了Shopify的CEO托比亚斯·卢特克上节目，他也是个有阅读障碍的人。但我们当时没深入讨论这个话题。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: There's an amazing amount of entrepreneurs who are dyslexic. And I attribute it back to the fact it's because we couldn't get jobs. We just went to create our own thing because we had to figure out our own way to work.
turns.zh: 有很多成功的创业者都有阅读障碍。我认为这源于他们无法找到合适的工作，只能自己开创事业，因为他们必须找到适合自己的工作方式。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's a bittersweet feature maybe.
turns.zh: 是啊，这或许是个喜忧参半的特质。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah. I think that... Whenever I meet somebody with a disability and they talk about the disability, I quickly go, "What's your super ability?" Tell me what it's because somebody who's blind can hear things that are just unbelievable. They can smell things. They can smell people walking in the room, just crazy, crazy stuff. And you start to realize, I know that you don't have sight, but the reality is it's actually affected you in another way. And what does that superpower and how do we actually leverage that superpower?
turns.zh: 是的。每当遇到有残疾的人谈论自己的残疾时，我都会迅速问：“你的超能力是什么？” 比如，盲人能听到令人难以置信的声音。他们能闻到气味，甚至能感知到房间里走动的人的存在，真是太不可思议了。你会意识到，虽然他们看不见，但残疾实际上以另一种方式影响着他们。那么这种超能力是什么？我们又该如何有效利用它呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I want to touch on two more things before I let you go that I think are going to be helpful to a lot of people. One is being a founder, the other is just getting into alignment with what you're doing in life. So from the perspective being a founder, you told me that people actually can use this framework we've been talking about to decide if they should even be founders. What is your advice there?
turns.zh: 好的。在结束本次访谈前，我想再谈两点内容，我认为这对很多人都会有所帮助。一是关于如何成为一名创业者；二是如何在生活中找到自己的定位。首先，从创业者的角度来看，你告诉我，人们可以利用我们之前讨论的框架来判断自己是否适合成为创业者。你对此有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Part of it is to realize as a founder, you have to do a lot of different things. And so part of it is I think self-awareness is one of the biggest assets you're going to have. And to know what you you're good at, to know what you suck at, it's also going to tell you about the team. You need to build around you. And so to realize at some point, there's a lot of people who say they want to be a founder, but what I would tell you is when you start to realize what you're good at, what's your strengths, what do you suck at, what are your energy drains? (01:15:22): And then go talk to a couple of founders, you'll start to realize how to shape for you to be a founder and whether for you, you decided I'm on my own, I'm going to do this myself, and I can hire people on contracting, but I want no employees. And so you start to realize how do you want to shape this thing based on who you are? And you took the time to do that. But most people, they have this notion of being a founder, but they don't know what founder they want to be. And what I would tell you is that there are a whole bunch of different kinds of founders and that you should self awareness and knowing energy drivers and drains and the reason why you want to be a founder become paramount to actually your success.
turns.zh: 其一，作为创业者，你需要处理许多不同的事务。因此，自我认知是你最宝贵的财富之一。你要清楚自己擅长什么，哪些方面需要改进，这也能帮助你组建团队。某个时刻你会发现，有很多人声称想成为创业者，但我要告诉你，当你开始审视自己的长处、短处，以及耗费精力的因素时（01:15:22），去和几位创业者交流后，你会逐渐明确如何塑造自己的创业身份，以及是否应该独自创业、外包任务、但拒绝雇佣员工。最终你会发现，这一切都取决于你自身的特质。若你花时间深入思考，你就能找到适合自己的发展路径。但大多数人对创业者这个角色存在误解，却不清楚自己想成为怎样的创业者。我要强调，创业者有多种类型，自我认知、明确能量来源与消耗因素，以及明确创业初衷，这些都对成功至关重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so the advice there is look at your energy drivers and drains and also talk to founders, the interview prototype interviews to understand what it actually is and make sure you actually want to be doing that.
turns.zh: 因此，我的建议是审视自己的能量来源与消耗因素，并与创业者交流，通过访谈原型来理解创业者的真实面貌，确保你的选择符合自身需求。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Because what's interesting is I would say, so I've done two startups in the last year, so this is my eighth, and ninth startup. And what I realized is if I had go back to when I did my first startup, I spent more time on the logo and the website and all these other things that literally both of them, neither one has a website yet. It doesn't matter, right? I'm building the product, I got to make it a short works. And so you start to realize, you just realize there's different things you need to do. And what happens is you confuse activity with productivity and you end up doing a lot of work that just doesn't matter and you're stressing yourself out for all the wrong reasons. And so part of it is getting to be self-aware of those kinds of things is really important.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，我过去一年参与了两家初创公司（这是我的第八家和第九家创业项目），回顾时发现，如果让我重返第一家创业公司的初期阶段，我会把更多精力投入到设计logo、搭建网站等环节，但如今这两家公司至今仍未建立网站。这真的无关紧要，对吧？重点在于产品开发，必须以最短的时间产出可用的产品。由此可见，创业者需要专注于核心任务，而非徒劳的琐事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of being self-aware, last question is around getting back into alignment with yourself. You also tell me that people use this to deal with overwhelm and understanding and solve their career course.
turns.zh: 说到自我认知，最后一个问题是关于如何与自我重新建立连接。你还提到人们可以通过这个框架应对焦虑、明确方向、规划职业发展。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: I didn't build it for this reason, I didn't build it for this reason, but there was a point in November where I was just overwhelmed. I was literally like, come on, this is not what I want to do. This is, and there's just so many things pulling on me and pressing on me that I'm like, okay. And I like, you know what? I'm going to go take the test. So when job moves, there's some resources and there's a test you can take and it'll tell you which quest you're in. So it asks, you pushes and pulls and puts it together and then tells you the probability that you're in one of the four quests. And as I did it, I went through it and just said, this is where I'm at, this what's going on? This is what's pushing me, this what's pulling me, where should I go next? (01:17:46): And it says, you need to have realignment. So basically it was a realignment job and I realized, okay, what are the five things that are really pulling me out of alignment? It was like all these podcasts I had to do. I wasn't building product, I was promoting more. I was doing all these things that I had to figure out how to sell books to big companies, all this stuff that just isn't me. And I realized, screw it. I'm going to buy the books. I'm going to give them away. I'm going to do, I was able to actually look at that list and pull the things off my list and basically either not do them or delegate them to somebody else. And it was actually about me pulling myself back into alignment. So I actually had more energy, and to be honest, I woke up the next day, I was a young entrepreneur again. (01:18:28): And so it's this aspect of realizing why do I want to get out? Why do I want to take the next step? What is the next step? Well, then how do I frame the next step and take it? And so to be honest, I'm now using it as almost like a, not daily, but once a month I'll take it just to actually help me realize what's going on. And it's helped me stop the energy that's pulling me in one direction or another and helps me stay on track. And it's just a really cool tool to do that. And so I have a couple of colleagues who are doing it as well, and it just is interesting how they realize I'm not a very good delegator, but when I realized it affects my motivation this way, it's like all of a sudden I've become a way better delegator to say, these are the things that are just pulling me or are misaligning me.
turns.zh:
我这么做不是因为这个原因，我这么做不是因为这个原因，但11月的时候我真的不堪重负。我当时就想，拜托，这不是我想做的。有太多事情在拉扯我、压迫我，我觉得，好吧。我就想，知道吗？我还是去参加考试吧。所以当工作变动时，会有一些资源和测试，你可以参加测试，它会告诉你处于哪种状态。所以它会问你，推拉各种东西，然后告诉你处于四种状态中的一种。当我做这个测试时，我经历了整个过程，然后就说，这就是我的现状，到底怎么回事？是什么在拉扯我，什么在压迫我，我接下来该往哪走？（01:17:46）然后它说，需要重新调整状态。所以基本上这是一次状态调整，我意识到，好吧，有五件事真正让我偏离了正轨？都是那些我必须做但又不喜欢的播客。我不是在做产品开发，而是在做推广。我在做所有这些事情，比如如何向大公司推销书籍，所有这些根本不符合我的风格的事情。我意识到，去他的，我要买书。我要把书送人。然后我就能做了，实际上我能看看那份清单，把那些事情从清单上划掉，要么不做，要么委托别人去做。这实际上就是把自己拉回正轨的过程。所以我现在有了更多的精力，说实话，第二天醒来，我又成了一个年轻的创业者。
（01:18:28）所以关键在于意识到为什么我想走出舒适区？为什么我想迈出下一步？下一步是什么？然后如何规划下一步并付诸行动？说实话，我现在每月都会做一次这个测试，帮助自己清醒地认识到正在发生什么。它帮助我阻止了那些把我往一个方向或另一个方向拉扯的能量，让我保持正轨。这真是一个很棒的工具。我有几个同事也在用它，有趣的是，他们意识到我不是一个很好的授权者，但当我意识到这会影响我的积极性时，突然间我就成了一个更好的授权者，可以说，这些事情就是在拉扯我，或者让我偏离正轨。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is so funny. Okay, so I know you finished the book in November, so I imagine that was related to your role.
turns.zh: 哇，太有趣了。好吧，我知道你11月完成了书稿，所以我猜这和你的角色有关。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: It was all about the law to the book. And it's like my whole thing is that the book was done and it was like then the publisher put all this... They put so much pressure on you to do all these other things and they have no data to tell you how well the book's going to do or not going to do it. And I'm like, it's done. Just get it out there. And they're like, no, no, no. We got to presale. We got to do this. You got to do all this promotion. And I'm like, "Thank God I had two other authors to help me with that load." But I mean, we had an article in HBR, had the idea cast, they were on Wall Street Journal. I don't know any of that stuff. I get intimidated by all that stuff. So it's like like, okay, you guys take that stuff. But still, I had to do a lot of different speaking. And I love to do this because I know the people, I know your audience, I know what to do, but talking about HR to HR people is scary to me.
turns.zh: 这完全和法律相关。关键是书已经完成了，但出版商却给你施加了各种压力，让你做这些其他事情，而且他们没有数据告诉你书会卖得好还是不好。然后我说，书已经完成了，赶紧发布吧。他们说，不，不，不。我们要预售，要做这个预售，要做这个推广。我就说，谢天谢地，我还有两个其他作者帮我分担这些工作。但我的意思是，我们在《哈佛商业评论》上发表了文章，想法被采纳了，登上了《华尔街日报》。但这些我都不懂。我被这些东西吓到了。所以我就想，好吧，你们负责这些吧。不过我还是得做很多不同的演讲。我喜欢做这些，因为我了解听众，了解你们的受众，知道该怎么做，但对HR人群讲HR相关的内容对我来说很可怕。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't think they would be happy with what you've shared today necessarily.
turns.zh: 我觉得他们未必会对您今天分享的内容感到满意。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah. I'm sure we're going to get some, just so you're clear, we're probably going to get some backlash from some of it as well. But again, I am looking at it as I am trying to make progress for the masses here and I think that the advice I'm trying to give should be able to help. It's not going to help everybody, but it should help a lot of people.
turns.zh: 是啊。我确定我们会收到一些反馈，坦白说，可能还会有一些负面评论。但话说回来，我现在致力于为大众创造价值，我相信我提供的建议应该能有所帮助。虽然不能帮助所有人，但应该能帮助很多人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I love that it helped you in your own struggle when you were about to launch this book. That's so awesome.
turns.zh: 而且当您即将推出这本书时，它对您自己的奋斗历程有所帮助。这真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: That was a surprise. That was a little bonus.
turns.zh: 真是个惊喜。这算是个额外的小惊喜。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Ultimate dot pruning. And I know you also built a product and just to give you opportunity to plug this, there's a product that you are building launching that is this book as a product. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 最终的精简处理。我知道您还开发了一款产品，借此机会宣传一下，您正在开发并即将推出的产品，就是把这本书作为一个产品。能讲讲吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: So we're in the very early stages of it. We're doing some things where it's going to facilitate asking the questions, and then it's got some AI to help build and summarize your situation. It'll actually take and help summarize your energy drivers and drains, and then as you prototype, you'll provide feedback. It'll provide context back to that to basically help you pick the prototype or pick the area that you want to really focus on. And so we're in the midst of fleshing that out. It probably won't be ready until the fall, but the reality is we're in early stages of it. I've got probably a couple hundred people in data testing it out and just working through it, but at some point when it comes out, I'll make sure I reach back out and let you know where it is and you can attach it to it.
turns.zh: 我们目前还处于初期阶段。我们正在开发一些功能，方便用户提问，然后通过人工智能帮助分析和总结用户的情况。它会收集并总结用户的能量驱动因素和消耗因素。然后在原型设计阶段，用户可以提供反馈，系统会根据反馈调整，最终帮助用户选择合适的原型或重点关注的领域。目前我们正在完善这些功能。产品可能要到秋季才能正式上线，但实际上，我们现在还处于早期阶段。已经有几百人参与数据测试和体验，但正式发布后，我会及时告知大家进展，方便大家关注。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, got it. Before we get to where to buy the book and all these things, is there anything else, Bob, that you wanted to share or you think is valuable to leave us today?
turns.zh: 好的，明白了。在我们讨论购买书籍等事项之前，鲍勃，还有什么想和我们分享或认为对大家有价值的信息吗？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: No, you hit it all. You're an amazing interview. I really appreciate you taking the time to do this. At some point I felt like I might've fed them with a fire hose, so some people might have to listen to it twice. I talk too fast, I get excited, but I think we hit all the big spots. Thank you. Awesome.
turns.zh: 没有了，您已经把所有重点都讲到了。您真是位出色的嘉宾。非常感谢您抽出时间接受采访。有时候我感觉自己讲得太快，信息量太大，可能有些人需要听两遍。我确实讲得太快了，但我觉得我们已经把所有关键点都涵盖了。谢谢，太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The ultimate compliment I get from people is I have to listen to this one on 1X speed.
turns.zh: 我收到的最高赞誉就是有人说他们不得不以1倍速听这个访谈。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah. I think I got that. I got that one when we did the one on jobs, speed done was like, yeah, I listened to most of it at one and a half. I had to listen to this one at one.
turns.zh: 是啊，我懂您的意思。我记得之前做关于求职的访谈时，大家反馈说他们以1.5倍速听了大部分内容。这次这个访谈他们只能听1倍速。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yep, too funny. Okay, and then where can folks find the book if they want to?
turns.zh: 太有趣了。好的，那么如果大家想买这本书，可以在哪里找到呢？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Amazon is where you... Amazon borders, all the big book retailers you can find it. It's called Job Moves:9 Steps for Making Progress in Your Career Yep. There we go.
turns.zh: 亚马逊平台，以及所有大型书店都可以找到。书名是《Job Moves：9个步骤助你事业进步》。没错，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I got one here too.
turns.zh: 我这里也有一本。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: And to be honest, my thing is you can also go to jobmoves.com and it has basically free resources to basically help you walk through the process, steps themselves. And so if you go to jobmoves.com, it'll, there's a test to tell you what Quest you're in. There's a form for doing the interviews. There's a form basically to help you with prototyping, et cetera.
turns.zh: 老实说，你也可以去jobmoves.com，那里有基本免费的资源，可以帮助你逐步完成整个流程。只要访问jobmoves.com，就能进行测试，判断你处于哪个阶段。还有填写表格用于面试准备，以及原型设计等功能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Actually have Jobmoves.com, I was checking the book to make sure you had the right domain. That's a great domain.
turns.zh: 实际上我有jobmoves.com，我之前检查过书稿，确保你用对了域名。这是个很棒的域名。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: We did, we did. We worked hard. Well, to be honest, it was one of the reasons why we named the book the way it was because the domain was available.
turns.zh: 确实，我们付出了很多努力。说实话，我们之所以给书取这个名字，也是因为当时域名还空着。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you had read, you were originally going to call this book, Hire Your Next Job or something like that.
turns.zh: 我记得你之前说过，原本想把书命名为《Hire Your Next Job》之类的。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, yeah. Actually, if you go into my Dropbox and you look at it's called My Next Thing. It was really about helping people find their next thing. But in the end, the publisher had to have influence on it, of course. And so I think I'm happy with Job Moves. I think it's a good thing. What's interesting is we can't... Hiring your next job was very inside job Jobs-to-be-Done pun kind of thing. But the reality is you had to be inside Jobs-to-be-Done, to get the pun, so it didn't really make sense to other people outside it. So it is what is.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。实际上，如果你去我的Dropbox看看，书名叫《My Next Thing》。最初的初衷是帮助人们找到下一个目标。但最后出版商肯定有自己的考量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Go for that big tam.
turns.zh: 去拿那块大肉吧。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, I guess that's exactly right.
turns.zh: 是啊，我想这确实没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bob, this is incredible. Thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 鲍勃，这太棒了。非常感谢你能来参加节目。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Thank you.
turns.zh: 谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think it's going to be helpful to a lot of people, so thank you.
turns.zh: 我觉得这本书会对很多人有帮助，所以谢谢你。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Thank you, Lenny. Thank you so much for your time. And if they want to reach out to me, please, LinkedIn is the best place to go. And what I would say is one favor I could ask your listeners is that I'm a very curious person and I love to solve struggling moments, and so I might regret saying this, but the reality is if you have a struggling moment that you've been struggling with for a long time and you have no solution to help you figure it out, drop me a line so I can actually start to accumulate some of these struggling moments to figure out where I should go next.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。非常感谢你抽出时间。如果听众想联系我，最好通过LinkedIn。说实话，我特别想请求听众帮个忙。我是个很好奇的人，喜欢解决难题，但说起来可能不太合适，但现实是，如果你有长期困扰却又找不到解决方案的难题，欢迎联系我，这样我就能开始收集这些难题，思考下一步该怎么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a very generous offer. What's the best way to reach out? You said on LinkedIn?
turns.zh: 这真是太慷慨了。联系方式是什么？你说在LinkedIn上？

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: LinkedIn, and just LinkedIn messaging. I'll accept the invite, or you can do it in message. It doesn't matter. But LinkedIn is the best way. I get too many emails and I have a very specific process around how I manage LinkedIn. That's just very useful for me.
turns.zh: LinkedIn就行，通过消息发送就行。我可以接受邀请，或者你也可以直接发消息。都行，但LinkedIn是最好的方式。我收到的邮件太多了，而且我对如何管理LinkedIn有很严格的流程。这对我来说非常有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. I'm glad you answered the question I forgot to ask, which is how listeners can be useful to you. So thank you for doing that.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。很高兴你回答了那个我忘了问的问题，就是听众如何能对你有所帮助。谢谢你这么做。

turns.speaker: Bob Moesta
turns.en: Yeah, yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bob, thank you so much.

turns.en: Thanks, Lenny.
